title: Hand and Upper Extremity Fellowship
level: Independent advanced clinical-physician-fellowship self-study curriculum (not fellowship training)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.level: Advanced postgraduate physician self-study for learners who have completed orthopaedic or plastic surgery residency, or comparable prior knowledge.
requiredKnowledge: Ability to read primary guidelines and critically evaluate evidence
prerequisites.institutionalPrerequisiteContext: These academic prerequisites mirror the level, not admission rules. The actual JHU clinical fellowship is one year and requires completion of orthopaedic or plastic surgery residency; it states board eligibility at fellowship start.

objectives: Map presenting signs to hand/wrist/elbow anatomy and a defensible differential.
Interpret common upper-extremity imaging and identify uncertainty/associated injury.
Synthesize board blueprint domains with dated authoritative guidelines and distinguish cognitive review from supervised clinical care.
Describe the principles and complications of bone/joint, tendon, nerve, vascular, skin/wound, congenital, rehabilitation and general topics.
Use ethical, safe, source-aware decision explanations and communicate that course assessments are not validated certification predictors.

units.title: Foundations: functional anatomy, examination, and imaging
objectives: Relate compartmental anatomy to motion, sensation, tendon excursion, vascular territories and examination findings.
Use a repeatable hand/wrist/elbow exam and document neurovascular status; identify limitations of plain films and advanced imaging.
topics: surface anatomy; flexor/extensor apparatus; intrinsic muscles; median/ulnar/radial nerves; vascular arcades; standard wrist/hand projections; structured examination
units.casePractice: Label anatomy on a public normal wrist case; submit a one-page focused examination checklist.
units.assessment: Practical: 5-point rubric (anatomic correctness, exam sequence, localization, imaging interpretation, safety documentation).

units.title: Acute hand and wrist trauma: fractures and dislocations
objectives: Classify common hand, carpal, distal forearm and elbow injuries using standard views and pattern language.
Prioritize open injury, compartment/vascular threat, instability and time-sensitive referral; compare options without treating a classification as an automatic operation.
topics: metacarpal/phalangeal; distal radius/ulna; scaphoid/carpal; perilunate; DRUJ; elbow; pediatric physeal; reduction/imaging principles
units.casePractice: Write a radiograph-first differential and escalation plan using AO reference classification pages; do not download images.
units.assessment: Case rubric: injury identification, instability/associated injury, urgency, evidence/uncertainty, follow-up contingencies.

units.title: Fracture healing, malunion, nonunion, and reconstruction
objectives: Explain biology and biomechanics of fracture healing, grafting and osteotomy at a conceptual level.
Analyze articular congruity, rotation, alignment, fixation constraints and complications.
topics: bone biology; bone graft; delayed/nonunion; malunion; distal radius corrective osteotomy; osteonecrosis; infection
units.casePractice: Prepare a comparison matrix for deformity, symptoms, imaging, goals and limitations of reconstructive options.
units.assessment: Written rubric: mechanism, relevant anatomy, alternative explanations, treatment objective, complication surveillance.

units.title: Joint, ligament, and wrist instability
objectives: Distinguish degenerative, inflammatory, post-traumatic and infectious joint presentations.
Describe ligament-based wrist stability and interpret common instability patterns, including scapholunate and DRUJ/TFCC topics.
topics: scapholunate and lunotriquetral ligament
TFCC/DRUJ instability
degenerative, inflammatory, post-traumatic and infectious arthritis
contracture and stiffness
units.casePractice: Use a hidden-diagnosis Radiopaedia wrist/case link only where lawful; create findings-to-differential table without copying images.
units.assessment: Scoring: findings, localization, differential, confirmatory evaluation, uncertainty statement.

units.title: Tendon injury, reconstruction, and compartment syndromes
objectives: Localize flexor/extensor injury from zone, tendon function and mechanism.
Explain repair/reconstruction principles, rehabilitation dependency and warning signs for compartment/ischemic injury.
topics: flexor tendon zones and repair/reconstruction
extensor tendon injury, mallet and boutonniere
tenosynovitis and tendinopathy
compartment syndrome and Volkmann sequelae
units.casePractice: Create a fictional tendon injury handoff and rehabilitation questions; no procedure steps or unsupervised competence.
units.assessment: Rubric: functional anatomy, examination, injury classification, priorities, rehab coordination and limits.

units.title: Peripheral nerve, compression neuropathy, and brachial plexus
objectives: Localize median, ulnar and radial neuropathies from sensory/motor findings and distinguish overlapping lesions.
Summarize compression, nerve injury, repair/graft/transfer, neuroma and plexus assessment at board-cognitive level.
topics: median, ulnar and radial nerve localization
CTS/cubital tunnel and other compression
acute/chronic injury, neuroma, graft and transfer
brachial plexus and neuromuscular conditions
units.casePractice: Submit a localization diagram plus CTS-6-guideline decision explanation; distinguish what the source supports from practice variation.
units.assessment: Rubric: localization, discriminating findings, appropriate tests, guideline use, differential and caveats.

units.title: Vascular injury, ischemia, and replantation principles
objectives: Recognize vascular compromise and identify urgent escalation concepts without providing a treatment order set.
Describe revascularization/replantation decision factors and relevant anatomic/ischemic considerations.
topics: vascular anatomy and perfusion assessment
arterial injury, thrombosis, embolism and aneurysm
chronic ischemia/vasospasm
replantation/revascularization decision concepts
units.casePractice: Analyze fictional mechanism/exam descriptors; produce a safety and escalation checklist and identify unanswered questions.
units.assessment: Rubric: vascular concern, time-critical recognition, uncertainty, referral/escalation, no invented thresholds.

units.title: Skin, wounds, fingertip, nail, coverage, and infection
objectives: Classify common wounds, nailbed/fingertip trauma, burns, bites and injection/extravasation injury.
Compare principles of coverage, wound healing and infection assessment; separate educational planning from clinical management.
topics: fingertip and nailbed trauma
coverage, graft/flap concepts and wound healing
bites, envenomation, infection and burns
injection/extravasation injury
units.casePractice: Write a short evidence map for an open wound scenario using AO/ASSH source links, preserving institutional protocols as local.
units.assessment: Rubric: wound characterization, host/context, contamination/infection concern, options/limitations, safety.

units.title: Benign/malignant lesions and Dupuytren disease
objectives: Construct a differential for common masses and lesions; identify features warranting further diagnostic evaluation.
Explain Dupuytren disease and contracture in the published board domain without oversimplified treatment certainty.
topics: benign masses and bone lesions
skin tumors, sarcoma and metastasis
Dupuytren disease/contracture
diagnostic evaluation and referral limits
units.casePractice: Create a fictional mass workup map distinguishing history/exam/imaging/pathology decisions.
units.assessment: Rubric: differential breadth, red flags, diagnostic sequence, referral, citation quality.

units.title: Arthritis, congenital/pediatric hand, and neuromuscular conditions
objectives: Compare common hand/wrist arthritides and describe impairment-oriented evaluation.
Recognize congenital patterns and pediatric/neuromuscular conditions explicitly listed in the ABOS blueprint.
topics: hand/wrist degenerative and inflammatory arthritis
contractures, stiffness and osteonecrosis
pediatric and congenital hand patterns
neuromuscular disorders and syndrome associations
units.casePractice: Prepare an age-sensitive case comparison matrix, including referral and rehabilitation issues.
units.assessment: Rubric: age/context, domain mapping, functional goals, differential, respectful communication.

units.title: Rehabilitation, prosthetics, pain, complications, and safety
objectives: Explain the team role of therapy, orthoses, prosthetics and functional outcome measures.
Recognize stiffness, CRPS/pain, DVT, medication/safety, and postoperative complications as cognitive topics, not authorization to treat.
topics: orthoses, prostheses and hand therapy
stiffness, pain syndromes and CRPS
complication/safety review and medication reconciliation
functional outcomes and team-based recovery
units.casePractice: Create a discharge/rehabilitation counseling outline from a fictional case, with patient-specific decisions deferred to the treating team.
units.assessment: Rubric: function, team coordination, red flags, risk communication, access/equity.

units.title: Professional practice, ethics, research literacy, and board blueprint integration
objectives: Apply consent, professionalism, communication, evidence appraisal and patient safety to educational scenarios.
Map all 7 ABOS weighted categories and all ABPS domains; explain that blueprints differ and no question bank predicts passage.
topics: consent, professionalism and communication
patient/physician safety
study design and evidence appraisal
ABOS and ABPS blueprint crosswalk and exam limits
units.casePractice: Complete a source critique and blueprint map; state what the published material does not establish.
units.assessment: Rubric: source hierarchy/date, correct domain map, evidence limits, ethics, clear nonclinical disclaimer.

assignment.title: Integrated hand and upper-extremity evidence portfolio
assignment.instructions: Across one fictional case each from trauma, nerve/tendon, joint/ligament, and wound/vascular content, make a one-page evidence map: problem representation, localization/classification, differential, missing information, relevant primary source/guideline date, relevant board domain, risks/uncertainties, referral/team considerations, and what cannot be concluded. Use externally linked authentic de-identified educational cases only under their rights terms; fictional written scenarios are clearly labeled.

rubric.criterion: Source quality, recency and accurate attribution
Safety, uncertainty, ethics and referral limits

assignment.passingInterpretation: Formative feedback only; not validated, board-endorsed, clinical competency evidence, or proof of exam readiness.

components: 10 original, sourced multiple-choice questions with keyed explanations
12 unit retrieval tasks and source critique
Learner self-audit mapping confidence and uncertainty
assessment.scoringPlan: Formative 100-point rubric: practice questions 20%, unit assignments 30%, portfolio 40%, source/version audit 10%. No cut score, predictive validity, official exam content or guarantee of passing has been established.
assessment.safety: No treatment advice for a real patient, no procedural authorization and no patient-specific inference.

studyHours.planType: Transparent independent study plan; planned rather than delivered time.
studyHours.currentStatus: Only verified ready time is current public external media listed below; the 36-hour recorded lecture target is not met. The plan is an educational allocation, not a claim of institutional teaching hours or clinical training.

topicGaps: Actual accessible, unique, duration-verified recordings total 3.942778 hours; 32.057222 hours remain below the 36-hour video target. Scripted episodes and planned clips do not count as rendered time.

Recordings offer selective orientation rather than full coverage. Major domains still lacking a verified long-form lecture sequence include carpal/metacarpal/phalangeal and pediatric trauma breadth; fracture healing/infection and scaphoid biology; wrist ligament/DRUJ/TFCC instability; tendon reconstruction and rehabilitation; vascular injury/replantation; wound coverage, bites and infection; masses/tumor; congenital/pediatric anomalies; arthritis; prosthetics/therapy; ethics/safety and evidence appraisal.

The new brachial-plexus and forearm-malunion recordings are academic grand rounds, not clinical protocols; verify any dated treatment discussion against current authoritative sources. The short 8:47 tendon overview is supplementary breadth only.
Distal-radius CPG full-text fetch cited in the source packet encountered an automated PMC challenge; no specific recommendation from that inaccessible text is newly asserted here.

Johns Hopkins public sources confirm the one-year ACGME-accredited fellowship and prerequisite residency but do not disclose proprietary didactic timetable, clinical volumes or learner assessment rubric. Human clinician review of this independent self-study expansion has not been performed.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: This is an ACGME-recognized physician fellowship specialty area. Johns Hopkins identifies its one-year fellowship as ACGME accredited. medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Johns Hopkins says fellows must be board eligible at entry and graduates are eligible to apply for the hand certification examination through their individual board; this self-study curriculum creates no eligibility, credential or case-list credit. Check ABOS and ABPS rules for the specific applicant/year; do not infer automatic or dual-board certification.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This packet covers only the Johns Hopkins physician hand and upper-extremity fellowship named in the supplied item packet. It is not a generic directory category or research/nonphysician supplemental degree. Institution name and original item-packet URL are preserved; the official school-wide directory entry and current departmental programme page were both checked. The Johns Hopkins page describes a cross-department training model, not a separately advertised combined primary board program. The independent online course is not the Johns Hopkins course.
sourceCaveats: Official JHU public programme pages confirm ACGME accreditation, duration, broad rotations and board pathway; no unpublished institutional curriculum was inferred.
ABOS 2025 blueprint is the only weighted board blueprint used; ABPS content is mapped in its own categories without invented weights.
The word “fellowship” denotes a physician graduate clinical training programme at JHU. The delivered artifact is independent self-study, not institutional training or credentialing.
Current board rules may change; use each board’s primary current instructions for any real application. The ABPS and ABOS timing change does not waive the primary certification/case requirements.

topicGaps: Actual accessible, unique, duration-verified recordings total 3.942778 hours; 32.057222 hours remain below the 36-hour video target. Scripted episodes and planned clips do not count as rendered time.

Recordings offer selective orientation rather than full coverage. Major domains still lacking a verified long-form lecture sequence include carpal/metacarpal/phalangeal and pediatric trauma breadth; fracture healing/infection and scaphoid biology; wrist ligament/DRUJ/TFCC instability; tendon reconstruction and rehabilitation; vascular injury/replantation; wound coverage, bites and infection; masses/tumor; congenital/pediatric anomalies; arthritis; prosthetics/therapy; ethics/safety and evidence appraisal.

The new brachial-plexus and forearm-malunion recordings are academic grand rounds, not clinical protocols; verify any dated treatment discussion against current authoritative sources. The short 8:47 tendon overview is supplementary breadth only.
Distal-radius CPG full-text fetch cited in the source packet encountered an automated PMC challenge; no specific recommendation from that inaccessible text is newly asserted here.

Johns Hopkins public sources confirm the one-year ACGME-accredited fellowship and prerequisite residency but do not disclose proprietary didactic timetable, clinical volumes or learner assessment rubric. Human clinician review of this independent self-study expansion has not been performed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which nerve traverses the carpal tunnel with the flexor tendons?

options.text: Median nerve
Ulnar nerve
Superficial radial nerve
Posterior interosseous nerve

practiceQuestions.rationale: The median nerve and nine flexor tendons traverse the tunnel; ulnar nerve/artery are outside it in Guyon canal. [Stanford anatomy video]

practiceQuestions.stem: A pattern of numbness in the small finger and ulnar half of the ring finger should primarily prompt which reasoning step?

options.text: Assume CTS and proceed directly to release
Broaden localization to the ulnar nerve and other lesions
Diagnose radial neuropathy without exam
Exclude neurologic causes

practiceQuestions.rationale: Ulnar sensory distribution is not the median nerve territory of CTS; localize and assess alternatives. [Stanford anatomy; AAOS CTS guideline]

practiceQuestions.stem: What does the 2024 AAOS CTS guideline say about CTS-6?

options.text: It is never useful
Strong evidence supports CTS-6 to diagnose CTS in lieu of routine ultrasound or NCV/EMG
It mandates nerve conduction tests in every case
It confirms diagnosis from radiographs

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline strongly supports CTS-6 in lieu of routine ultrasound or electrodiagnostic testing; uncertainty may still support further testing.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which ABOS 2025 hand blueprint domain is weighted at 15%?

options.text: Bone
Nerve
Circulatory system
Skin/fascia/nails

practiceQuestions.rationale: The published weights are bone 20%, joint/ligament 20%, muscle/tendon 13%, nerve 15%, circulatory 7%, skin/fascia/nails 12%, general/other 13%.

practiceQuestions.stem: How should the clinician use a CT in a complex distal-radius injury in a case-based discussion?

options.text: Always order it in every wrist injury
Consider whether additional imaging may clarify fragments or alter the operative plan; follow current evidence and context
It replaces plain radiographs and examination
Use it to guarantee an outcome

practiceQuestions.rationale: Use decision-oriented, case-specific imaging reasoning; the current local guideline and specialist evaluation govern. AO provides fracture-pattern references; AAOS/ASSH guideline should be consulted, but full PMC text was blocked during this research and no exact threshold is claimed.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which prerequisite residency does Johns Hopkins list for its hand fellowship?

options.text: Neurology or emergency medicine
Plastic surgery or orthopaedic surgery
Radiology or pathology
General practice only

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official JHU page describes a one-year fellowship for surgeons completing plastic surgery or orthopaedic surgery residency.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which distinction is accurate about hand fellowship versus hand certification?

options.text: The fellowship itself is a board examination
The JHU program is a one-year ACGME fellowship; a separate board subspecialty exam/certificate pathway exists, with eligibility and case requirements
Every graduate automatically becomes certified
Self-study confers eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: JHU says eligible to apply through their board; ABOS describes examination, case-list and primary certification requirements. No automatic award.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the correct reuse approach for a Radiopaedia case in an independent course?

options.text: Copy all images to course storage because viewing is free
Link to the case; if reproducing an image, comply with its CC BY-NC-SA terms and Radiopaedia modifications, provide attribution, and avoid large-scale reuse
Remove author attribution
Assume all page text and imagery have identical unrestricted rights

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia permits limited educational reuse under modified attribution/noncommercial/share-alike terms for contributor images, not wholesale copying; link-only is the conservative course policy.

practiceQuestions.stem: A suspected tendon injury causes loss of active flexion in a fictional vignette. What should a board-cognitive learner do first?

options.text: Name likely tendon/zone using examination and mechanism, consider associated injuries, and state limits
Assume the tendon is intact if passive motion is full
Perform a repair based on a video
Ignore neurovascular documentation

practiceQuestions.rationale: The blueprint includes flexor tendon injury/reconstruction; structured assessment and associated-injury reasoning are educational objectives, not procedural authorization.

practiceQuestions.stem: An educational chapter or recording recommends an approach but is older than a current guideline. Which approach is strongest?

options.text: Prefer the older video without checking
Date-check against current board/primary guideline sources and state evidence limits
Treat it as an institutional protocol
Assume the video represents JHU private didactics

practiceQuestions.rationale: Older media may be useful for concepts but recommendations need comparison against dated current sources; no private JHU didactic content was accessed.

title: Orthopaedic Surgery Residency
prerequisites: Medical-school-level anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology and clinical reasoning; foundational OpenStax chapters are suitable for review, not professional preparation.
Read English-language clinical guidance and distinguish guideline scope from a patient-specific plan.
No prerequisite conveys admission or eligibility for medical school, residency, fellowship, licensure or board examinations.
objectives: Map basic science, imaging and clinical data to ABOS Part I domains.
Build structured differentials for common adult and pediatric musculoskeletal problems.
Recognize urgent escalation issues while keeping educational case discussion distinct from patient care.
Critically appraise guideline populations, recommendation scope, dates, limitations and evidence quality.
Use freely linked, authentic case resources within their access and rights limits.
Explain that a course, credential, treatment observation or video does not confer procedural competence or board eligibility.

topicGaps: General-principles/basic science: core anatomy, physiology, biomechanics and evidence-appraisal instruction remains incomplete; only one short hand-infection lecture plus focused grand rounds are available.
Adult spine: only one mixed-topic long-form recording; broad degenerative, trauma, deformity, infection and tumor coverage is insufficient.

Trauma: acute compartment syndrome and fracture-related infection receive focused grand-round discussion, but polytrauma, open fractures, fracture classification, fixation/healing and complications lack comprehensive verified lecture coverage.
Upper extremity: one shared-decision lecture and hand-infection recording do not provide comprehensive shoulder, elbow, wrist, nerve, tendon, vascular and fracture teaching.
Lower extremities/reconstruction/foot and ankle: focused ACL/meniscus lectures do not cover the breadth of arthroplasty, hip, ankle, foot, deformity, infection, complications and rehabilitation.
Pediatrics: focused ACL and Perthes talks leave growth, pediatric trauma, developmental hip, deformity, safeguarding and other pediatric conditions substantially undercovered.
Neoplasms: one tumor-surgery prophylaxis trial lecture is not comprehensive bone/soft-tissue tumor diagnosis, imaging, staging, biopsy planning or treatment teaching.
Broad board-blueprint synthesis and evidence literacy: public lectures are selected topical talks, not a full ABOS/AOBOS blueprint-aligned course or validated exam preparation.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Research packet identifies Johns Hopkins School of Medicine’s Orthopaedic Surgery Residency. Because the broader contract requests exact Harvard-affiliated variants, HCORP and its four named participating Boston teaching hospitals are included as one combined programme with site variants, not as separately verified residencies. Johns Hopkins public overview lists six clinical sites. Programme rotation descriptions are not complete official curricula. Hopkins page does not display a specific ACGME status; public directory verification was inconclusive. HCORP official page expressly describes ACGME approval. All materials here are independent and unaffiliated.
sourceCaveats: Hopkins page confirms the named five-year residency and public curriculum but does not state its program-specific current ACGME accreditation status; public ACGME directory lookup did not yield a direct record.
HCORP page states ACGME-approved and names four major hospitals; its public curriculum page did not extract, so no schedule beyond the about page is represented.
AAOS 2025 compartment-syndrome guideline is adult acute traumatic-extremity scope and explicitly cautions against pediatric extrapolation; verify recommendations in full source at use.
AAOS major-extremity-trauma SSI guideline is dated 2022 and has stated population exclusions; check later updates before use.

One free external NewYorkOrtho lecture is counted only by duration displayed next to its exact title in public YouTube search/playlist results; other media runtimes remain unknown. No YouTube media was downloaded.
Northwestern case pages and MedPix provide access to authentic educational case material; no case image, real-patient data or record copied. No blanket reuse rights inferred.
Public content can be removed, changed, geo-restricted or made login-only. Re-check runtime/access before future use.
No human clinical review performed; date-sensitive care decisions require qualified clinician review and current official guideline sources.
No claims of guaranteed exam performance, eligibility, licensure, affiliation, credited training, patient-care competence, case volume or operative proficiency.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is asked what information should anchor a musculoskeletal problem representation before choosing a diagnosis. Which approach best reflects sound reasoning?

options.text: Name the imaging abnormality as the diagnosis without considering symptoms.
Combine location, tempo, mechanism, function, examination and relevant imaging while stating uncertainty.
Choose the most common diagnosis and omit alternatives.
Select an operation before collecting clinical information.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOS Part I tests diagnostic problem-solving using clinical information, laboratory data and imaging. A concise representation integrates clinical context rather than treating an image as a diagnosis. This is an original educational question, not an official item.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult with a recent lower-leg injury develops worsening pain and increasing concern on serial examination. Which action best reflects a safety-first learning response?

options.text: Reassure because distal pulses remain palpable.
Promptly escalate for urgent clinical reassessment of possible acute compartment syndrome; do not rely on a single absent/present sign.
Wait until the next routine clinic visit.
Apply a tighter circumferential dressing.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The current AAOS acute compartment syndrome guideline addresses adults with traumatized extremities. Suspected acute compartment syndrome is an urgent clinician assessment problem, not a self-study diagnosis or a situation to defer. The question avoids assigning an isolated sign as diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a public clinical practice guideline, which interpretation is most defensible?

options.text: Apply every recommendation to all ages and all related conditions.
Check population, scope, exclusions, publication date and recommendation strength before applying it.
Treat the publication date as irrelevant.
Use the guideline as a substitute for patient-specific assessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2025 AAOS compartment-syndrome CPG explicitly limits scope to adult traumatized extremities and excludes pediatric/adolescent and chronic exertional disease. Population, date and scope are essential qualifiers.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional open extremity fracture case is used in a classroom. Which resource is the strongest starting point for a current evidence-oriented discussion of prevention of surgical-site infection after major extremity trauma?

options.text: The AAOS 2022 prevention CPG, while checking its exclusions and current local guidance.
A patient story video with no references.
An isolated case report treated as universal policy.
A guideline on already established infection assumed to cover all prevention questions.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AAOS identifies a 2022 CPG specifically addressing interventions and risk factors for SSI after major extremity trauma, with stated exclusions; it is the appropriate evidence entry point, not a universal protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement accurately describes AO Surgery Reference as a course reading?

options.text: AO states that adult, pediatric and periprosthetic orthopedic trauma references are freely accessible; that does not automatically grant unrestricted rights to rehost its illustrations.
All content is public domain.
Every linked surgical technique is authorization for unsupervised practice.
AO content replaces accredited residency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AO confirms free access to several fracture-management reference sections and notes a large illustration collection. View access and reuse permission are different, and the reference does not create clinical competence or replace supervised training.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional child has an injury near a growth plate. Which reasoning priority is most important compared with an otherwise similar adult injury?

options.text: Ignore skeletal maturity because pediatric bone is identical to adult bone.
Account for age, growth plate and remodeling potential while assessing alignment and safeguarding context.
Apply adult guideline recommendations without checking population.
Assume every child fracture represents abuse.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The pediatric domain requires developmental anatomy and growth-aware interpretation. An individualized assessment includes mechanism/history and safeguarding when appropriate, without automatic conclusions.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has a bone lesion identified during evaluation of pain. Before an unplanned excision or biopsy, what educational principle should guide the next discussion?

options.text: Plan the diagnostic approach with appropriate musculoskeletal oncology expertise because biopsy trajectory and tissue diagnosis can affect subsequent care.
Remove the lesion without planning to learn its histology.
Assume every lesion is benign based on one image.
Delay all evaluation until symptoms resolve.

practiceQuestions.rationale: A suspicious lesion belongs in a deliberate diagnostic and referral pathway. This question teaches planning and uncertainty, not a specific biopsy technique or a diagnosis from a fictional image.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement distinguishes primary orthopaedic board certification from ABOS hand and sports credentials?

options.text: ABOS lists Hand and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine as subspecialty certificates in addition to primary orthopaedic surgery certification.
Every fellowship creates a new primary specialty board.
Completion of a self-study course confers board eligibility.
The certificates replace primary certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOS states that it offers two subspecialty certificates—hand and sports—while primary certification has its own residency and Part I/Part II path. Fellowship/course enrollment alone confers no board status.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which description matches the current published ABOS Part I content organization?

options.text: General Principles, Adult Spine, Upper Extremities, Lower Extremities, Pediatrics and Neoplasms.
Only operative technique.
Only orthopedic trauma.
The twelve units in this independent course.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABOS blueprint identifies six reported domains in this organization and also provides a subspecialty-organized view. Course units map to, but do not reproduce or predict, the secure exam.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about the separate AOBOS pathway is supported by its current public exam page?

options.text: The American Osteopathic Board of Orthopedic Surgery has its own written examination pathway and exam content outline.
AOBOS is another name for the ABOS Part I exam.
The AOBOS page states that the ABOS and AOBOS award a single shared board credential.
This course grants eligibility for either board.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official AOA certification portal separately describes an AOBOS orthopedic surgery written exam and clinical exam pathway. Eligibility is determined by the board, not this course.

assignment.title: Integrated fictional-case portfolio
assignment.instructions: For four published link-out case prompts (one otology/imaging, one sinus or skull base, one adult neck mass/oncology, one pediatric or airway), write de-identified educational reasoning memos. Use no real patient record or copied image. Each memo states one-sentence representation, prioritized differential, data to seek, safe referral/urgent considerations, evidence date/population, uncertainty and patient communication plan. Include one research appraisal and a short reflective board-domain map. Do not issue a patient-specific treatment plan.

coveredTopics: BPPV, Ménière disease, vestibular migraine, vestibular schwannoma, facial nerve palsy, temporal-bone trauma, audiovestibular testing; neurotology is a fellowship/subcertification path, not this residency’s separate board.

unitMap.text: Rhinology, allergy and anterior skull base
coveredTopics: Acute/chronic rhinosinusitis, nasal polyps, allergy, epistaxis, smell loss, orbital/intracranial complications, CT anatomy, endoscopic sinus and skull-base principles.

unitMap.text: Head and neck oncology, unknown primary and neck mass
coveredTopics: Oral cavity/oropharynx, larynx/hypopharynx, salivary glands, thyroid, nodal levels, HPV-associated disease, unknown primary, pathology/radiology and survivorship.

unitMap.text: Pediatric otolaryngology and congenital disorders
coveredTopics: Otitis/effusion, hearing loss, congenital ear/nasal lesions, tonsil/adenoid disease, pediatric airway, dysphagia, pediatric neck/thyroid/skull base, child safety.

unitMap.text: Laryngology, voice, airway and swallowing
coveredTopics: Laryngeal anatomy/physiology, vocal fold motion, benign lesions, dysphagia, aspiration, tracheostomy care, airway stenosis, voice/swallowing testing.

unitMap.text: Facial plastics, trauma, reconstruction and sleep surgery
coveredTopics: Facial trauma, rhinoplasty principles, facial nerve rehabilitation, reconstruction, sleep-disordered breathing, DISE concepts, surgical outcome trade-offs.

unitMap.text: Thyroid, parathyroid, salivary and endocrine head-neck surgery
coveredTopics: Thyroid/parathyroid disease, salivary gland masses/infection, facial nerve anatomy, neck dissection concepts, voice outcomes.

unitMap.text: Emergency ENT, perioperative care and patient safety
coveredTopics: Airway, epistaxis, deep neck infection, foreign body, otologic emergency, postoperative bleeding, antibiotics/analgesia, consent, deidentification and safety.

unitMap.text: Sleep medicine and upper-airway surgery
coveredTopics: Sleep testing concepts, airway anatomy, nonsurgical management context, DISE, palatal/skeletal/pediatric options, tonsil surgery, outcomes and shared decision-making.

unitMap.text: Research, quality, ethics and lifelong board learning
coveredTopics: ACGME competencies, quality improvement, morbidity/mortality, evidence-based practice, patient-reported outcomes, research pathways and board assessment.

topicGaps: Observed unique free specialty-recording runtime is 7.739722 h, below the 36.0-h floor. Residual verified gap is exactly 28.260278 h (1,695.6167 minutes; 1,696 planned production minutes when rounded up). The added 1:33:18 GGR is counted once; original scripts, planned episode minutes, and inaccessible material add zero ready hours.

Video-topic gaps remain: detailed general ENT examination/anatomy; temporal-bone and broad otology; comprehensive audiogram interpretation and hearing-loss mechanisms/rehabilitation; vestibular disorders beyond the existing hearing talk; adult and pediatric rhinology/allergy and complications; laryngology/voice/swallowing/airway; head-and-neck oncology, unknown primary, thyroid/parathyroid/salivary; pediatric ENT; facial plastics/trauma/reconstruction; emergency/perioperative care; evidence, ethics, quality and research literacy. New long-form recording covers sleep-surgery strategies but does not provide systematic coverage of these domains.

The publicly linked lectures are selective grand-rounds/conference sessions, not comprehensive residency teaching. No eligible new full-length recording with observed duration was verifiable for most domains in this expansion window; candidate playlist metadata extraction was blocked by YouTube rate-limit/403 responses. That access limitation is not evidence the content does not exist.

Detailed current 2026 ABOHNS Written Exam and future 2027 OTE blueprint domains/weights remain behind the physician portal; no login or bypass was attempted. This packet retains a broad public ACGME/ABOHNS domain crosswalk, not an official weighted exam blueprint.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

boardNames: American Board of Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery (ABOHNS) — primary specialty certification
medical.boardStatus: A distinct primary physician specialty with ABOHNS primary certification. The OTE is a practice examination, not a separate certification exam. Primary certification uses Written and Oral Exams after accredited training and eligibility review. Separate ABOHNS subspecialty certifications include Neurotology, Sleep Medicine and Complex Pediatric Otolaryngology; they are not separate residency tracks or boards in this course.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Independent self-study does not satisfy ACGME accredited residency, board-specific eligibility, case collection, peer review, examination, state licensure or certification requirements. Check ABOHNS and current eligibility rules directly. No exam outcome is guaranteed.

officialProgrammes.name: Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery (OHNS) Residency Training Program — Clinical Track
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official overview describes the Clinical Track as five years with six months research and two residents/year. The institutional rotations page lists five-year track rotations, multiple hospital/ambulatory sites and progressive clinical exposure. Johns Hopkins directory lists ACGME Accredited and total 5–6.5 years across variants.

officialProgrammes.name: Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery (OHNS) Residency Training Program — Research Track (NIH-funded R25/T32 descriptions)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: A physician residency research track, not a research-only non-physician programme and not a separate specialty/board. The overview describes a six-year research track with 18 months NIH-funded research; the rotations page describes a T32/24-month research opportunity, six ACGME-accredited months and clinical time extending to PGY6. Public schedule pages vary; exact current track schedule requires institutional confirmation.

officialProgrammes.name: Harvard Medical School / Mass Eye and Ear / Mass General Brigham Otolaryngology–Head and Neck Surgery Residency Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory-listed institutional variant; a full internal rotation or lecture curriculum was not verified in the directory discovery.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exact official institutional title preserved. Johns Hopkins lists two tracks inside its OHNS physician residency: clinical and research. The research track remains an OHNS residency with research time; it is not relabelled as a separate fellowship or board specialty. Official directory claims ACGME accreditation for the listed residency, while ACGME requirements below are standards, not the programme curriculum. Public Hopkins overview (5/6 years), rotation schedule (R25/T32 and PGY5+) and directory (5–6.5 years) contain different schedule descriptions; retain rather than reconcile without current institutional confirmation. Research/fellowship timeline is not an independent training equivalence claim.
sourceCaveats: Johns Hopkins directory publicly identifies this named OHNS residency as ACGME Accredited and lists 5–6.5 years; the dedicated program overview and rotations page give differing pathway duration descriptions. Individual current track schedule should be confirmed with Johns Hopkins; no schedule was invented.
ACGME 2025 requirements describe national program standards, not Hopkins-specific teaching hours, operations performed, resident case volume or individual competence.

ABOHNS announced on 2025-12-03 a new Written Exam blueprint implementation in 2026 and OTE blueprint implementation in 2027. Detailed current blueprint files are available through a physician portal; this task did not log in or bypass access. The domain map uses only public high-level board descriptions and ACGME requirements.

Clinical guidance checked 2026-10-07. AAO-HNSF adult sinusitis guideline was published 2025; adult neck-mass guideline is 2017, sudden hearing loss 2019, pediatric tonsillectomy 2019 and pediatric tubes 2022. Check source pages for newer updates before clinical use.

Stanford/AAO-HNSF videos are linked, not copied. Exact player runtimes were observed statelessly on public watch pages on 2026-10-07. For two long conference recordings only explicitly delimited clinical-talk/Q&A segments were counted; nonlecture introduction/dissection/closing time excluded. Deduplicated by unique video IDs.

Radiopaedia/publication case pages are authentic published case resources as represented by their source. Free-to-view does not guarantee course republication rights; links only, no images, slides or patient records copied. The course has not independently audited source anonymization.
AAO-HNSF site terms restrict external copying/transfer including AI-based uses; reading links direct learners to official source material, and no page content or video media is rehosted.

The course is independent and unaffiliated. Human clinical review is not performed. It does not provide accredited GME, affiliation, medical degree, supervised patient experience, licensure, procedure competence, board eligibility, certification or guaranteed passing.

medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 54-year-old has a lateral neck mass persisting for three weeks without a clear infectious history. Which course best follows the purpose of the adult neck-mass guideline?

options.text: Assume a reactive node and repeat empiric antibiotics until it disappears.
Promptly perform risk-informed evaluation, appropriate targeted examination and diagnostic testing/referral rather than allowing an unexplained mass to drift without follow-up.
Proceed directly to open excision in every case.
Use the pediatric neck-mass guideline because all masses are alike.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO-HNSF guideline targets efficient, accurate initial work-up of adult neck masses to avoid delay in diagnosing potentially malignant disease; it is not for children and does not require open biopsy for every mass. Empiric antibiotics are not a substitute when bacterial infection is not supported.

practiceQuestions.stem: An adult reports abrupt unilateral hearing loss beginning yesterday. What is the most appropriate first reasoning priority?

options.text: Wait several months because unilateral symptoms usually resolve.
Promptly distinguish conductive from sensorineural loss with appropriate examination and audiometric assessment, then use the current sudden-hearing-loss pathway.
Order routine laboratory panels as a complete substitute for hearing assessment.
Assume age-related hearing loss.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2019 AAO-HNSF update aims to promote prompt recognition and management of sudden sensorineural hearing loss. Establishing the type and severity of loss guides appropriate next steps; details should be checked in the guideline rather than inferred from a single symptom.

practiceQuestions.stem: A child with recurrent acute otitis media has no middle-ear effusion at the candidacy assessment. Which choice is consistent with the 2022 tympanostomy-tube guideline?

options.text: Recommend tubes solely because the episodes were recurrent.
Do not recommend tubes for recurrent AOM without effusion at the assessment; reassess the clinical situation and discuss alternatives.
Perform a cochlear implant.
Treat all children with prophylactic antibiotics indefinitely.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline page provides a specific FAQ addressing recurrent infections without persistent fluid, and the 2022 update covers children 6 months–12 years considered for tubes. Confirm exact recommendations in the source and apply to the child’s context.

practiceQuestions.stem: A caregiver asks whether a child should have tonsillectomy after four documented throat-infection episodes in the past year. What is the best evidence-based response?

options.text: Every child with four episodes should undergo immediate surgery.
Review the current guideline’s episode-count thresholds, modifiers and watchful-waiting recommendations before making an individualized shared decision.
Tonsillectomy is never appropriate in children.
Use the adult sinusitis guideline.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2019 pediatric tonsillectomy guideline covers children 1–18 years and explicitly addresses indications and natural history. A count alone is not enough to bypass the full criteria, modifying factors, risks and caregiver discussion.
practiceQuestions.domain: Pediatric surgical management and shared decisions

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician is asked whether the 2025 adult sinusitis update can be applied to a pediatric patient without qualification. Which answer is most accurate?

options.text: Yes; the AAO-HNSF page states its target patients are adults and identifies a 2025 update, so pediatric care requires age-appropriate guidance.
Yes; all age groups are interchangeable.
No guidance for children exists.
Use the guideline as a diagnostic test.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO-HNSF describes the 2025 guideline as adult sinusitis guidance; it should not be silently extrapolated to children. Verify current pediatric-specific recommendations separately.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is the correct interpretation of the Otolaryngology Training Examination (OTE) in ABOHNS’s certification system?

options.text: It is a separate board certification exam that awards primary certification.
It is a recommended practice test; primary certification separately requires Written and Oral Exams after accredited training and eligibility.
It is a surgical simulation credential.
It guarantees passing the Written Exam.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOHNS describes the OTE as a practice test and primary certification as a process with Written and Oral Exams. Passing the OTE does not grant certification or eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 34-year-old adult with a new neck mass has no fever or focal bacterial symptoms. Which initial plan best avoids a preventable diagnostic delay?

options.text: Empiric antibiotics solely for the presence of a mass, with no planned reassessment.
Risk-informed work-up under the adult neck-mass guideline, including appropriate targeted examination and specialist follow-up.
Reassure without an examination.
Order tests unrelated to history or examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The adult guideline aims for accurate, efficient work-up and prompt diagnosis where malignancy is possible; treatment for infection should be grounded in clinical signs rather than used as an untracked delay.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement most accurately describes Johns Hopkins’s published OHNS resident tracks?

options.text: Clinical and research tracks are separate specialties with different boards.
The programme describes clinical and research tracks within the same OHNS residency; the research pathway adds research time and public pages differ on exact timeline details.
The research path is a non-physician PhD programme.
Both are fellowships after residency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Johns Hopkins public pages describe distinct clinical/research pathways inside the OHNS residency; the overview and rotations page describe research duration differently. This course preserves the variance rather than inventing a single schedule.

practiceQuestions.stem: When teaching with a Radiopaedia imaging case under its published license, what is the safe default for a course that has not obtained case-specific permission?

options.text: Copy the images without attribution because they are free to view.
Link learners to the case; if an image is reused, verify applicable terms, attribution and non-commercial/share-alike conditions before use.
Assume all third-party cases are public domain.
Remove attribution to protect privacy.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Radiopaedia says the licensing page and Terms of Use govern. Its CC BY-NC-SA license permits compliant noncommercial reuse with attribution and share-alike, but free viewing alone is not blanket permission. Link-only avoids unnecessary copying.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best describes the evidence supporting this independent course?

options.text: It is accredited residency and qualifies learners for ABOHNS certification.
It is self-study mapped to public standards; it does not replace supervised clinical training, licensure, board eligibility, certification or validated exam preparation.
Completing all cases grants procedure competence.
The questions are official ABOHNS exam items.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME residency includes progressive supervised clinical experience, competency assessment and structured education. An independent curriculum cannot grant training, licensure or board status; all practice items are original educational questions, not official exam content.

title: Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Independent Residency Program
level: Clinical physician residency — independent pathway-aligned independent study
prerequisites: Advanced physician-level foundations in surgical anatomy, physiology, pathology, pharmacology, wound biology, perioperative care, evidence appraisal and clinical ethics.
Learners should already know basic surgical terminology; the course does not provide foundational MD/DO education.
Applicants to actual independent residency need an ABPS-accepted prerequisite surgical pathway; exact pathway conditions change and must be checked in the current ABPS Booklet of Information.
Do not use this course for patient-specific treatment, unsupervised procedures, prescribing, credentialing or claims of clinical competency.
objectives: Distinguish the Hopkins independent physician residency, the joint institutional program context, other pathways, ABPS certification, and the limits of public curricular data.
Organize specialty study using the ABPS published content outline, without claiming that the course reproduces proprietary board materials.
Explain core wound repair, tissue transfer, microsurgical, regional reconstruction, aesthetic, perioperative, ethical and evidence-appraisal concepts.
Analyze fictional educational vignettes by separating observations, missing data, alternatives, uncertainty and escalation needs.
Use current authoritative guidelines and identify their scope and limits.
Recognize that independent self-study is not accredited training, supervised clinical experience, licensure, board eligibility or procedural competence.

unitMap.text: Scope, prerequisites, professionalism, and evidence
Wound biology, assessment, and closure principles
Grafts, local/regional flaps, and tissue transfer
Microsurgery, replantation, nerve and lymphatic reconstruction
Hand and upper-extremity reconstruction
Craniofacial, cleft, and maxillofacial reconstruction
Breast reconstruction and implant safety
Burns, scar management, and reconstruction
Skin/soft-tissue tumors, oncologic reconstruction, and lower extremity/trunk
Aesthetic surgery, biomaterials, and patient-centered selection
Perioperative medicine, anesthesia, critical events, and complications
Evidence appraisal, ethics, QI, and oral/written synthesis

topicGaps: Five eligible unique specialty recordings total 4.951111 hours, leaving 31.048889 hours below the 36-hour video floor; no foundation or supplement hours are credited.
Public playlist and UCSF video-page runtimes are not available in fetched evidence; candidate video access remains to be verified item by item.

The ABPS outline includes broader categories requiring further free video evidence: anesthesia and critical care, pathology, oncology, congenital craniofacial conditions, breast, aesthetic surgery, implants, microsurgery, hand, burn/scar, soft-tissue tumors, ethics and complications.
Original clip plans below cover topical gaps but are planned only and contribute no verified hours.

One newly added UCTV wound-healing lecture has a conservative duration observation from the final full-page transcript timestamp (6861.99 seconds, rounded down); the player total runtime was not separately exposed. Recheck it if exact player runtime is required.
Full narration has been authored for six source-grounded episodes; all are scripted, not rendered, and contribute zero video hours. Existing originalClipPlan entries remain plans only.

Insufficient verified free lecture coverage remains for anesthesia/critical care, pathology and oncology depth, aesthetic techniques and biomaterials, microsurgical technical instruction and complications, lower-extremity/trunk/genital reconstruction, and broad craniofacial trauma. Several topics have reference sources but no eligible duration-verified lecture.

boardNames: American Board of Plastic Surgery (ABPS): Written Examination and Oral Examination are required components of the certification process, subject to current eligibility and Board requirements.
Underlying prerequisite surgical specialty board status/certification may be required depending on pathway and training history; verify current ABPS Booklet of Information.

boardStatus.status: Johns Hopkins directory and departmental source identify an ACGME-accredited three-year independent physician residency. ABPS maintains plastic-surgery certification and separate written and oral examinations. Independent is a training model, not a different specialty board or board examination. A candidate’s actual eligibility requires qualifying prerequisite training, requisite training and current ABPS determination.
boardStatus.blueprintScope: This course is organized to the ABPS Written Examination Content Outline revised May 2023 and the published ABPS Written Examination Blueprint; the outline organizes cognitive topics, while the Board alone controls exam construction. This course is not an official review product or pass predictor.
boardStatus.eligibilityNotice: Do not infer admission, ABPS eligibility or certification from course completion or the JHU directory listing. The ABPS 2026–27 Booklet of Information and the Board’s application-year rules control; prerequisite pathways and individual histories matter.

medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Independent educational self-study does not create ABPS or other board eligibility, certification, accredited training, licensure, procedural competence or supervision. ABPS has written and oral examination steps, and only ABPS determines a candidate’s eligibility under current rules. Confirm all current pathway details directly with ABPS.

officialProgrammes.name: Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Independent Residency Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory lists ACGME Accredited, three years, Johns Hopkins Hospital and Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center, and prerequisite surgery residency. Johns Hopkins department page describes the broader joint Johns Hopkins/University of Maryland residency and two pathways (integrated and independent), with additional clinical sites. No full independent rotation calendar or public didactic schedule was retrieved.

medical.programmeSourceScope: This packet’s exact listing is a clinical physician Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Independent Residency Program. The Johns Hopkins School of Medicine directory explicitly labels the entry “ACGME Accredited,” gives three years and names Johns Hopkins Hospital and Johns Hopkins Bayview. The Department’s own residency page describes one Johns Hopkins/University of Maryland residency with integrated and independent pathways and multiple Baltimore-area teaching sites; this is a partner/institutional variant of the same clinical training context, not evidence for a second independent award. The independent route is a physician residency after qualifying prerequisite surgical training, not a generic directory category, research fellowship, non-physician supplement, or combined independent/integrated course. The ABPS is the specialty certifying board; it has separate written and oral examinations. “Independent” is a training pathway, not a separate board exam. Eligibility is not established by this course and depends on current ABPS conditions, prerequisites, completed training, and Board determination. The Hopkins page says its program is ACGME accredited; the directory separately names ACGME Accredited. Neither page discloses a complete didactic lecture archive or detailed current rotation calendar. The JHU/UMD program page describes affiliated clinical sites and broad program facts but does not establish institutional affiliations for this independent curriculum.
sourceCaveats: YouTube PRSJournal playlist contains 21 unique entries. Four individually fetched pages displayed runtimes and “Watch full video” without an age restriction; these contribute 3.045 specialty hours. Two age-restricted entries and one unavailable entry have durations but are excluded; other entries lack verified runtimes.
The UCSF public videos page identifies topic headings but extracted page did not expose embedded video URLs, player runtimes, or free-access evidence; not counted.
ABPS written content outline retrieved is revised May 2023; the Board may update it. The ABPS 2026–27 booklet and Board web pages were checked 2026-10-07; future changes are possible.
ACGME 2025 program requirements and milestones describe accredited training/evaluation, not a self-study course or institutional curriculum disclosure.

Some NCBI/PMC endpoints displayed an access challenge in this environment. The course relies on the successfully read primary institutional, board, ACGME, ASSH, ABA and ACPA sources; no unviewed PMC text is treated as verified.
No real patient images, records, case details or proprietary exam content are copied into this curriculum. Public access is not permission to reproduce.
No human clinical review has been performed. Clinical care requires qualified clinicians using current sources, local resources and supervision.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has a chronic wound with delayed healing. Which study response is most appropriate?

options.text: Conclude that one mechanism is proven from appearance alone.
Describe the wound, identify missing perfusion/infection/nutrition/context data, build a differential, and cite source/date.
Select a definitive operation from a still image.
Assume all chronic wounds require a flap.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPS outline covers wound biology and management. A careful learner distinguishes observation from inference and requests context rather than claiming a diagnosis or definitive operation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about superficial burns and total body surface area is consistent with ABA guidance?

options.text: Superficial burns are included in TBSA by default.
Superficial burns are excluded from TBSA calculations; adult Rule of Nines is approximate and children need age-appropriate adjustment.
The adult Rule of Nines is equally accurate for infants.
Small burns to hands never merit consultation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABA states superficial burns are not counted in TBSA; adult Rule of Nines is a rapid estimate, and children require age-sensitive methods. Critical-area injury can merit specialty evaluation regardless of total area.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has multiple digit injuries with tendon involvement. Which response best matches ASSH/ACEP guidance?

options.text: Routine follow-up without consultation.
Immediate hand-surgery consultation or transfer if unavailable.
No specialist evaluation if skin is intact.
Manage based only on radiograph.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The May 2025 ASSH/ACEP guidance lists multiple-digit injuries with tendon and/or nerve involvement among conditions that may need immediate consultation or transfer. Local resources and bedside judgment remain important.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which response is the safest educational interpretation of a new change in a free flap monitoring signal?

options.text: Treat one isolated device reading as definitive proof of thrombosis.
Ignore changes because free flaps do not fail after transfer.
Recognize a possible complication, promptly escalate to the responsible microsurgical team, and integrate clinical assessment and trend/context.
Independently perform salvage surgery after reading a lecture.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABPS/ACGME curriculum includes monitoring and management of flap complications, while competence requires supervised clinical training. An educational signal is not a diagnosis or authorization for intervention.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best reflects the 2024 ACPA Parameters?

options.text: Cleft care is a single-operation episode.
Interdisciplinary team care and longitudinal evaluation are central, with transition to adult care addressed.
Plastic surgery alone determines all speech, hearing, dental and psychosocial needs.
A self-study curriculum can replace team evaluation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACPA frames care around an interdisciplinary cleft/craniofacial team and longitudinal needs, including transition to adult care. It is not replaced by a single specialty or self-study.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement is most accurate about the independent plastic-surgery pathway and certification?

options.text: It is a separate board specialty with no exams.
ABPS describes minimum requisite independent training, and candidates must meet prerequisite pathway conditions and current Board eligibility requirements.
Completing any online course makes a learner eligible for ABPS certification.
Prior board certification automatically waives all ABPS examination requirements.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPS has distinct training requirements and written and oral examinations; eligibility is subject to prerequisite path, training and current board rules. Independent is a training model, not a different plastic-surgery board.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional post-mastectomy discussion is most educationally sound when it:

options.text: Presents one reconstruction technique as universally best.
Coordinates with oncologic context, lays out reasonable alternatives and uncertainty, and centers patient goals.
Treats an implant as risk-free.
Defers discussion until after surgery.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPS content includes multiple post-oncologic reconstruction approaches; patient-centered choice depends on clinical and preference factors. This is a reasoning exercise, not personalized medical advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner scores highly on a self-study quiz about flaps. What does this establish?

options.text: Procedure competence.
ACGME milestone attainment.
Board eligibility.
Only performance on that assessment; it does not establish procedural competence, milestone level or board eligibility.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME Milestones are intended for evaluations in accredited programs, and assessment results in an independent course cannot confer clinical competence or eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a fictional child with a burn, which source-based caution is appropriate?

options.text: Use an adult Rule of Nines without adjustment.
ABA notes pediatric burns may benefit from burn-center referral for pain, dressing, rehabilitation, caregiver and other needs; use age-appropriate area estimation and clinician judgment.
Never refer if TBSA is small.
Use the course to make a transfer order.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABA guidance specifically notes pediatric referral considerations and the limits of adult TBSA rules. Referral is a clinical-team decision with local context.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is an appropriate use of the ABPS content outline?

options.text: Copy protected exam items to predict tested questions.
Use its published topic categories to organize lawful, original self-study and write original questions.
Claim course quiz performance proves ABPS readiness.
Treat it as a complete clinical practice guideline.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABPS publishes a content outline to describe domains; exam materials are confidential, and the outline is not a guideline or pass predictor.

assignment.title: Source-cited reconstructive reasoning memo
assignment.prompt: Select a fictional text-only vignette (burn referral, hand/limb defect, breast reconstruction context or head/neck defect). In 800–1,200 words state only supplied facts; list missing data; map to an ABPS domain and ACGME competency; compare three conceptual reconstruction categories without procedural instructions; discuss function, goals, trade-offs, source quality/date and consultation needs; conclude with an oral-case summary and what cannot be determined. Cite two current authoritative sources. No real patient data/images.
rubric: Problem, missing facts, anatomy and uncertainty (0–4)
Balanced options, patient goals, risks and team context (0–4)
Authority, source date and evidence appraisal (0–4)
Safety boundary, ethics and lawful use (0–4)
assignment.limitations: 20-point formative educational rubric only; no clinical competency judgment, valid exam cutoff or board-performance prediction.

assessment.format: Twelve unit formative checks; 10 original source-cited questions; case memo; optional mock oral reasoning prompt.
assessment.blueprintAlignment: Mapped to ABPS content outline (May 2023) and ACGME Plastic Surgery Requirements (effective 2026); published ABPS target percentages are not exact current-item weights.
assessment.limitations: Questions are original and not official ABPS items, protected content, validated exam items or predictors. No practical/procedural assessment.

topicGaps: 36-hour freely accessible, runtime-observed specialty-video floor remains unmet: 7.698611 verified specialty hours; residual is 28.301389 hours. Authored scripts and target production minutes are not rendered videos and count as zero.

Public lecture coverage improved for head/neck virtual planning, lymphatic/microsurgery, scarring/wound biology, cleft care, and breast reconstruction. No public video search established a full rotation-level curriculum or the full seven-year Hopkins didactic archive.
Unit 1: the open wound-healing review and UTSW lecture provide conceptual context, not a current practice protocol or complete resident-level core.

Unit 2: ABA referral guidance remains the authoritative current referral source; the existing resuscitation lecture is not a current burn protocol. No runtime-verified full current acute burn-management series was found.

Units 3–4: closure/graft/flap and physiology/monitoring content remains thin; available source outlines/case reports and microsurgery talks do not provide operative instruction or validated monitoring standards.

Unit 5: ASPS lists a skin-cancer reconstruction guideline, reaffirmed in 2026, but the public index is a summary and linked journal full text access varies; no full runtime-verified oncologic reconstruction lecture was added.
Unit 6: new cleft lecture and current ACPA parameters expand coverage, but do not replace clinical cleft-team follow-up or an operative curriculum.
Unit 7: the existing hand lecture is older; current ASSH/ACEP May 2025 guidance is a referral resource, not a diagnostic/procedural substitute.
Unit 8: head/neck planning content was added, but facial trauma, oncologic decision-making and functional reconstruction remain incompletely covered.

Unit 9: a prepectoral lecture was added, but recordings do not replace current cancer/radiation/genetics multidisciplinary recommendations; the official autologous flap guideline page points to a 2017 guideline.
Unit 10: trunk/genital/lower-limb reconstruction has no complete free runtime-verified lecture series; lymphedema recordings supply only a narrow conceptual subdomain.
Unit 11: lymphedema and head/neck microsurgical recordings add topic diversity but do not teach current technical microsurgery, replantation, nerve reconstruction or VCA immunology.
Unit 12: no public, runtime-ledgered series sufficed for aesthetic/outcomes/oral reasoning; the ABPS outline and process remain source mappings, not protected exam material.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician residency (Johns Hopkins integrated Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery; independent self-study course, not clinical training)
boardNames: American Board of Plastic Surgery (ABPS) — Plastic Surgery Initial Certification: written and oral examinations, after Board approval and completion of current pathway requirements.
medical.boardStatus: A distinct ABPS Plastic Surgery certification exists. The ABPS calls the written exam cognitive and the oral exam an assessment of reasoning, judgment and problem-solving; both are required for certification. ABPS states six years of requisite integrated plastic-surgery training; Hopkins lists its integrated program as seven years total, six clinical and one mandatory research year. These descriptions are not contradictory: one reports total institutional program length, the other minimum plastic-surgery training. Formal ABPS review/admissibility, current license, privileges and other requirements apply. No separate board exam is asserted for hand, burn, craniofacial or microsurgery generic tracks or the research year. Checked 2026-10-07.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This course grants no board examination eligibility/admissibility. ABPS requires its formal approval and current pathway, training, licensure and privilege requirements. Independent self-study does not confer ACGME/RCPSC training, medical degree/prerequisites, supervised case volume, operative competence, state license, ABPS eligibility/certification or a passing guarantee.

officialProgrammes.name: Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Integrated Residency Program
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory: ACGME-accredited, seven years total with six clinical years and a mandatory research year; intern clinical time spans general surgery, plastic surgery and related rotations. Department page describes the broader Johns Hopkins/University of Maryland program, clinical sites and distinct integrated/independent pathways. Public teaching page lists weekly grand rounds, core curriculum, research symposium, skills/anatomy labs and mock oral exams, not a full rotation-level syllabus or public lecture archive.

officialProgrammes.name: Plastic Surgery Integrated Residency
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory-listed institutional variant; a full internal rotation or lecture curriculum was not verified in the directory discovery.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exact packet variant: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine, Plastic and Reconstructive Surgery Integrated Residency Program. Departmental pages use the institutional context Johns Hopkins/University of Maryland Plastic Surgery Residency and describe integrated and independent pathways; only the packet-named integrated path is included. No Harvard or other institutional offering appears in this packet, so none is invented or added. This is a clinical physician residency, not a generic directory category, combined board programme or research-only postdoc. Its research year is inside the seven-year programme, not a separate board specialty.
sourceCaveats: Packet includes one Hopkins integrated physician residency. The department also describes the Hopkins/University of Maryland institutional context and independent track; variants are preserved, not merged.
ABPS is the certifying board. Written plus oral examinations are required. Formal board review and other requirements apply; course completion never makes learners eligible.
The linked ABPS blueprint labels Level I target percentages effective 2021 and warns these are not exact current exam representation. May 2023 content outline is latest directly verified.
ACGME 2026 document covers integrated and independent programs; its standards do not reproduce Hopkins private schedule.
Burn referral guidance states it supports and does not replace professional judgment; video resuscitation lecture is not current protocol.
Four public videos counted for specialty: complete runtime visible on individual YouTube pages fetched 2026-10-07. VCA lecture is listed separately as supplement. No access permanence promised.
Human clinical review not performed. Independent education does not confer affiliation, accreditation, training, licensure, board eligibility, certification or procedure competence.

The public case report is linked for authentic educational discussion; patient de-identification and figure reuse permissions were not independently audited, so no images/records are copied or rehosted.

Public lecture coverage improved for head/neck virtual planning, lymphatic/microsurgery, scarring/wound biology, cleft care, and breast reconstruction. No public video search established a full rotation-level curriculum or the full seven-year Hopkins didactic archive.
Unit 1: the open wound-healing review and UTSW lecture provide conceptual context, not a current practice protocol or complete resident-level core.

Unit 2: ABA referral guidance remains the authoritative current referral source; the existing resuscitation lecture is not a current burn protocol. No runtime-verified full current acute burn-management series was found.

Units 3–4: closure/graft/flap and physiology/monitoring content remains thin; available source outlines/case reports and microsurgery talks do not provide operative instruction or validated monitoring standards.

Unit 5: ASPS lists a skin-cancer reconstruction guideline, reaffirmed in 2026, but the public index is a summary and linked journal full text access varies; no full runtime-verified oncologic reconstruction lecture was added.
Unit 6: new cleft lecture and current ACPA parameters expand coverage, but do not replace clinical cleft-team follow-up or an operative curriculum.
Unit 7: the existing hand lecture is older; current ASSH/ACEP May 2025 guidance is a referral resource, not a diagnostic/procedural substitute.
Unit 8: head/neck planning content was added, but facial trauma, oncologic decision-making and functional reconstruction remain incompletely covered.

Unit 9: a prepectoral lecture was added, but recordings do not replace current cancer/radiation/genetics multidisciplinary recommendations; the official autologous flap guideline page points to a 2017 guideline.
Unit 10: trunk/genital/lower-limb reconstruction has no complete free runtime-verified lecture series; lymphedema recordings supply only a narrow conceptual subdomain.
Unit 11: lymphedema and head/neck microsurgical recordings add topic diversity but do not teach current technical microsurgery, replantation, nerve reconstruction or VCA immunology.
Unit 12: no public, runtime-ledgered series sufficed for aesthetic/outcomes/oral reasoning; the ABPS outline and process remain source mappings, not protected exam material.
