practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement distinguishes an ACGME standard from board content?

options.text: ACGME sets GME program standards; ABPS outlines exam domains.
ABPS accredits residency programs.
Hopkins rotation pages set exam items.
ACGME grants board certification.

practiceQuestions.rationale: These sources answer different questions.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional patient has suspected inhalation injury and a deep hand burn. ABA guidance supports:

options.text: Ignore transfer networks.
Immediate consultation with consideration for transfer, while preserving professional judgment.
Use TBSA alone.
No referral because adult.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABA guidance identifies suspected inhalation injury and deep burns at critical sites; it does not replace professional judgment.

practiceQuestions.stem: For a defect after tumor excision, what is the soundest educational framework?

options.text: Choose the largest flap first.
Select before defining function.
Describe defect, objectives, tissue, donor/recipient risks, patient goals and unknowns before comparing options.
A mandatory ladder sequence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Begin with defect and objectives; no universal procedure follows.

practiceQuestions.stem: What can a single published thumb reconstruction case establish?

options.text: The flap is best for all thumb defects.
It illustrates one decision context, not comparative efficacy or universal indication.
Images are free to reuse.
It guarantees its stated outcome timeline.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Case reports are authentic but context-bound; image reuse requires rights.

practiceQuestions.stem: A safe educational hand-injury assessment includes:

options.text: Only wound length.
Perfusion, sensation, motor/tendon, skeletal/soft tissue and escalation context.
Assume perfusion if alert.
Wait for a video before seeking care.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Assessment considers function and neurovascular structures; real care uses urgent local pathways.

practiceQuestions.stem: Reconstruction is discussed with hereditary breast cancer context. Safest framing?

options.text: Speaker preference is universal.
Integrate current oncology/radiation context, preferences and multidisciplinary review; lecture is not a guideline.
Ignore genetic context.
Radiation is irrelevant.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Review current guidance with the clinical team; no universal answer follows from a lecture.

practiceQuestions.stem: Why is surface color alone insufficient for online diagnosis of a threatened flap?

options.text: Perfusion never changes.
Assessment integrates findings and time-sensitive specialist examination; online media cannot diagnose a patient.
All color change has the same treatment.
Imaging resolves all questions.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Clinical assessment requires qualified direct evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: What does Hopkins public description of a mandatory research year mean?

options.text: Every resident has identical research.
It describes this institutional program, not every program or individual board eligibility.
It replaces clinical years.
It certifies research competence.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hopkins describes a seven-year institutional structure including a research year.

practiceQuestions.stem: ABPS blueprint targets accompanied by a warning about exact current exam should be used how?

options.text: Guaranteed item counts.
Broad study orientation, checked against current official ABPS content.

Combine with leaked questions.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is true about this course and ABPS eligibility?

options.text: Course completion grants eligibility.

title: Reconstructive Microsurgery Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (independent self-study curriculum; not a clinical fellowship)-aligned independent study

prerequisites.intendedLevel: Post-residency plastic surgeons and senior plastic-surgery trainees studying cognitive principles; other clinicians may use selected foundations but this is not clinical training.
assumedKnowledge: Plastic surgery fundamentals and wound healing
Clinical evidence appraisal and professional ethics
requiredBoundaries: Do not attempt procedures or patient management from these materials.
Learners must use local clinical protocols and supervised training for clinical practice.
No patient data, protected exam items or unlicensed figures are included.

objectives: Explain core reconstructive microsurgery principles and evidence-based decision concepts.
Map ABPS published cognitive domains to topics without claiming a separate microsurgery examination.
Compare reconstructive options using defect, functional goal, donor morbidity, recipient anatomy and patient preference as explicit dimensions.
Interpret free-flap monitoring signals with attention to measurement limitations and escalation boundaries.
Appraise open clinical studies and distinguish descriptive institutional volume claims from audited case requirements.
Communicate uncertainty and complications in a structured oral reasoning format.
Apply privacy, copyright, consent and ethics rules to published case materials.

units.title: Foundations, evidence, scope and candidacy
objectives: Distinguish free-tissue transfer, pedicled flaps, grafts, replantation and lymphatic/nerve microsurgery.
Frame reconstructive goals, alternatives, donor/recipient trade-offs, risk and shared decision-making without claiming one flap is universally best.
Separate institutional programme descriptions, accreditation, board examinations and independent study.
topics: Indications and reconstructive ladder; wound biology; physiology of flap perfusion; patient-centered goals; evidence hierarchy; candidacy and multidisciplinary planning.
units.boardDomains: Core microsurgery; flap physiology; wound repair; general principles
units.casePractice: A fictional post-oncologic defect is used to build a goal-oriented options matrix, explicitly leaving procedure decisions to the treating team.

assessment.method: Short written concept map plus 5-minute oral reasoning brief
rubric: Recognition of uncertainty, safety and escalation boundaries (0-3)
assessment.masteryNote: Formative educational feedback only; score is not validated or a proxy for technical or board competence.

units.title: Microvascular anatomy and donor–recipient relationships
objectives: Map the relevant arterial, venous and perforator anatomy from an openly published diagram or source.
Explain why venous outflow, pedicle geometry, donor morbidity and recipient-vessel quality matter.
Compare imaging and clinical-anatomic information while acknowledging variability.
topics: Vascular territories; perforators; pedicle length/caliber; recipient vessel selection; injury zone; donor site and functional morbidity; imaging caveats.
units.boardDomains: Microsurgery; flap anatomy; regional reconstruction
units.casePractice: Fictional lower-limb wound: compare two plausible tissue needs and identify missing vascular and patient data; no procedural recommendation.

assessment.method: Short written concept map plus 5-minute oral reasoning brief
rubric: Recognition of uncertainty, safety and escalation boundaries (0-3)
assessment.masteryNote: Formative educational feedback only; score is not validated or a proxy for technical or board competence.

units.title: Microsurgical equipment, ergonomics and simulation
objectives: Describe microscope/instrument setup concepts and ergonomic factors affecting motor control.
Design a simulation log with repeatable measures of task quality and error review.
Explain why simulation/video observation cannot confer operative competence.
topics: Microscope optics and orientation; micro-instrument handling; tremor and fatigue; ergonomic setup; deliberate practice; nonliving models; assessment boundaries.
units.boardDomains: Microsurgery technical aspects; human factors
units.casePractice: Analyze a fictional practice-session checklist; define skill metrics without asserting a clinical proficiency threshold.

assessment.method: Short written concept map plus 5-minute oral reasoning brief
rubric: Recognition of uncertainty, safety and escalation boundaries (0-3)

units.title: Anastomosis principles, patency and failure modes
objectives: Interpret educational depictions of end-to-end, end-to-side and coupler concepts at a cognitive level.
Identify categories of technical failure and explain why patency tests are imperfect.
Construct a supervised escalation discussion for suspected anastomotic compromise.
topics: Vessel handling concepts; intima/adventitia; sutures/couplers; thrombosis, spasm, kinking and tension; patency assessment limitations.
units.boardDomains: Microsurgery technical aspects; couplers; flap monitoring; failing flap
units.casePractice: From a fictional schematic, enumerate potential failure modes and data needed; not a hands-on task or operative manual.

assessment.method: Short written concept map plus 5-minute oral reasoning brief

assessment.masteryNote: Formative educational feedback only; score is not validated or a proxy for technical or board competence.

units.title: Free-flap selection and perioperative planning
objectives: Match defect requirements to broad tissue types and donor-site constraints.
Integrate recipient-vessel quality, pedicle geometry and comorbidities in a decision matrix.
Explain why published surgeon-specific preferences cannot be generalized without comparative evidence.
topics: Fasciocutaneous, muscle, bone, composite and perforator flaps; donor burden; imaging; anticoagulation context; planned backup options.
units.boardDomains: Free flap types; indications; perioperative management
units.casePractice: Fictional board-style planning case: rank information gaps and justify a nonbinding options matrix.

units.title: Breast and truncal reconstruction
objectives: Compare reconstructive goals, abdominal donor-site considerations, perforator-flap alternatives and implant/autologous pathways.
Interpret outcome evidence with attention to denominator, selection and follow-up.
Explain how oncologic treatment, preferences and co-management affect planning.
topics: DIEP/GAP/PAP/TUG concepts; implant and autologous approaches; secondary revision; donor morbidity; patient-reported outcome considerations.
units.boardDomains: Reconstruction; breast and trunk; flap selection
units.casePractice: Fictional scenario: build a shared-decision question list and interpret study outcomes without using a patient image.

units.title: Head-and-neck and skull-base reconstruction
objectives: Relate defect geometry and functional goals to broad reconstructive requirements.
Organize risk assessment for recipient vessel, airway/swallowing, prior treatment and postoperative monitoring.
Interpret complications literature without treating cohort outcomes as an individual prognosis.
topics: Oral cavity, pharynx, mandible and skull-base defects; osseous/soft tissue options; recipient vessels; complication mechanisms and salvage concepts.
units.boardDomains: Regional reconstruction; free-flap complications; microsurgery
units.casePractice: Fictional post-resection defect: present a multidisciplinary handoff and a complication differential; no treatment advice.

units.title: Extremity trauma, limb salvage and replantation
objectives: Distinguish coverage goals from limb-salvage decisions and identify time-sensitive multidisciplinary inputs.
Explain injury-zone and vascular disease concerns in recipient-vessel selection.
Discuss replantation/revascularization candidacy domains and rehabilitation goals without making an individual indication.
topics: Lower-limb trauma; open defects; recipient vessel status; end-to-side/end-to-end tradeoffs; replantation indications/contraindications; functional outcome.
units.boardDomains: Microsurgery for free transfer/replantation; upper/lower extremity domains
units.casePractice: Fictional trauma conference brief: identify missing data and list stakeholders before comparing coverage pathways.

units.title: Nerve, functional muscle and lymphatic reconstruction
objectives: Describe the biological and functional objectives of nerve repair/transfer and vascularized muscle transfer.
Compare broad lymphatic procedures and evidence limits without asserting guaranteed prevention or cure.
Use objective functional and patient-reported endpoints in an outcomes plan.
topics: Nerve injury physiology; graft/transfer; free functional muscle; lymphovenous bypass and lymph-node transfer concepts; imaging and patient selection.
units.boardDomains: Nerve repair; lymphatic suturing; regional reconstruction

units.title: Postoperative monitoring, complications and salvage reasoning
objectives: Compare bedside clinical examination and adjunct monitoring approaches, their strengths and blind spots.
Recognize educational patterns of venous/arterial compromise, hematoma, infection and systemic confounders.
Use a structured, rapid communication/handoff framework without prescribing care.
topics: Clinical checks; Doppler, ICG and adjuncts; buried flap limitations; false positives; escalation and return-to-theatre as clinical-team decisions; audit.

objectives: Appraise study design, selection bias, denominators, follow-up and generalizability.
Apply privacy, consent, licensing and equity principles to images, cases and education media.
Translate board-outline domains into a learning plan without implying board readiness.

objectives: Synthesize goals, anatomy, evidence, donor and recipient issues, monitoring and contingencies in a structured oral presentation.

Build a dated update plan for guidelines, board materials and institutional eligibility requirements.
topics: Cross-domain synthesis; complication back-up reasoning; shared decision-making; reflective practice; current board blueprint distinction.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One official BIDMC programme, preserved under the BIDMC name and its companion Harvard-affiliated programme-page styling “Peter Jay Sharp Microsurgery Fellowship Program.” These pages describe the same BIDMC/Harvard Plastic Surgery Residency clinical programme, not two separate institutional tracks. Fellowship is an actual physician postgraduate clinical fellowship, not a generic directory label, research-only postdoctoral job, or non-physician imaging/AI supplement. No separate ACGME microsurgery accreditation or board examination is identified in reviewed current sources. No Johns Hopkins/other institutional variant added because this packet names BIDMC only and this task is one specialty evidence set.
sourceCaveats: Institution pages are not accreditation records or official board documentation. The linked BIDMC page states a one-year fellowship; current specific match/eligibility details should be checked with programme administrators.

BIDMC page reports more than 150 microsurgical procedures annually; the HMS/BIDMC programme page reports more than 200. They do not explain counting methods, timeframes or fellow-specific case distribution. Preserve as source-specific descriptions only; not verified volumes or guarantees.
Public pages do not provide the complete institutional curriculum, rotation schedules, exact didactic hours, fellow-specific case logs or outcomes; no institutional curriculum is invented.

title: Spine Surgery Fellowship

prerequisites.recommendedLearnerLevel: Advanced medical/graduate-health-science independent learner; not an admissions path, clinical credential or substitute for medical school, residency or supervised fellowship.
knowledge: Foundational gross anatomy, neuroscience, biomechanics, pathology, clinical epidemiology and medical terminology.
Ability to read clinical guidelines and distinguish recommendation, evidence certainty, and individual decision-making.
No real-patient management, prescribing, supervised practice, or procedure performance is authorized.
prerequisites.safetyAndAccess: Use fictional cases only. Link to authentic de-identified external case resources; verify per-record license, do not copy/rehost images or patient records. Respect paywall, login, platform and publisher terms.
prerequisites.actualProgrammePrerequisiteBoundary: ACGME defines Orthopaedic Surgery of the Spine as a one-year fellowship. Institution entry prerequisites are not uniform: BIDMC public page requires completed orthopaedic residency and ABOS board eligibility/certification; Johns Hopkins describes orthopaedic or neurological surgery residency. This course verifies no applicant qualifications and grants no prerequisite credit.

objectives: Describe spine fellowship programme variants without treating institutional pages, accreditor requirements, and board examinations as interchangeable.
Use anatomy, imaging and neurologic localization to structure fictional differential reasoning and identify uncertainty.
Compare evidence across degenerative, deformity, trauma, infection, tumor, congenital/pediatric, perioperative and complex reconstruction topics.
Map educational objectives to published ACGME fellowship competency requirements and ABOS/ABNS core board boundaries; do not claim a spine-specific board examination.
Use source attribution, evidence appraisal, case-based reasoning and oral explanation in formative study only.

units.title: Scope, indications, consent, and longitudinal spine evaluation
objectives: Separate diagnosis, natural history, patient goals, and surgical indication in a structured discussion.
Describe limitations of examination/imaging and frame uncertainty without offering a patient-specific recommendation.
Explain the independent-study boundary and the roles of orthopaedic and neurological surgeons.
topics: spine fellowship identity; informed consent; shared decision making; functional measures; red flags; non-operative care; referral pathways
institutional variant comparison: programme page vs accreditor requirement vs certifying-board pathway
eligibility boundary and educational consent language; no independent credential or clinical privilege
boardDomains: ACGME Orthopaedic Surgery of the Spine: patient care, professionalism, communication, systems-based practice; ABOS/ABNS primary specialty knowledge only
units.casePractice: Fictional adult with axial back pain and intermittent leg symptoms: distinguish history/examination questions, red flags, missing data, and care-team escalation; no treatment plan.
units.assessment: Write a one-page scope-and-uncertainty map; rubric: separates evidence from inference (40%), communicates limits/escalation (30%), cites primary sources (30%).

units.title: Spinal anatomy, biomechanics, imaging, and neurologic localization
objectives: Relate vertebral, disc, neural, ligamentous, and vascular anatomy to common symptom patterns.
Compare what standing radiographs, CT, and MRI can answer and identify modality limits.
Localize a fictional neurologic pattern while preserving differential diagnoses.
topics: cervical/thoracic/lumbar anatomy; nerve roots; cord; sagittal/coronal balance; alignment parameters; imaging planes; degenerative findings vs symptoms
symptom–sign–imaging concordance and localization as separate inferential steps
standing full-length radiographs versus cross-sectional MRI/CT: distinct questions and limits
boardDomains: ACGME subspecialty-specific knowledge and imaging interpretation; ABOS/ABNS core orthopaedic/neurosurgery science
units.casePractice: Use only a published, license-checked teaching case (e.g. MedPix search) and a report; record the original source/license. No image export or inference beyond record.
units.assessment: Annotated conceptual anatomy map and modality-selection rationale, marked for accuracy, uncertainty and citations.

units.title: Degenerative lumbar disease: radiculopathy, stenosis, and evidence appraisal
objectives: Distinguish disc herniation, stenosis, spondylosis, and nonspinal mimics as differential categories.
Interpret a guideline recommendation with population, comparator, evidence quality, and outcome in view.
Discuss indications conceptually without turning a vignette into a clinical recommendation.
topics: lumbar radiculopathy; central/lateral-recess/foraminal stenosis; concordance; natural history; non-operative options; surgical evidence; complications
degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis evidence: decompression-alone versus fusion trial synthesis
patient-reported outcomes and applicability rather than single-image thresholds
boardDomains: ACGME subspecialty clinical knowledge and evidence-based practice; ABOS orthopaedic core
units.casePractice: Fictional MRI report with multiple degenerative findings: prioritize symptom/imaging concordance and list at least three alternatives; no diagnosis asserted.
units.assessment: Structured evidence appraisal worksheet scored for PICO, applicability, bias/limitations and no premature certainty.

units.title: Cervical spondylosis, myelopathy, and deformity
objectives: Differentiate a cord-syndrome pattern from isolated root symptoms in a written hypothetical.
Summarize current DCM guidance while distinguishing recommendation strength and population.
Identify why progression and examination changes warrant clinical assessment, not online self-triage.
topics: degenerative cervical myelopathy; radiculopathy; cord compression; approach-selection concepts; alignment; DCM guidelines
clinical myelopathy versus nonmyelopathic cord compression; population-specific 2017 recommendations
2025 AO Spine synthesis: conditional versus strong recommendations, and MRI signal limitations
boardDomains: ACGME orthopaedic spine competency; ABNS primary broad neurosurgery domains (no separate spine board exam)
units.casePractice: Fictional exam narrative and MRI report modeled as text only; students classify known/unknown and compare with open DCM guideline population.
units.assessment: Guideline comparison: recommendation, evidence certainty, included population and one limitation.

units.title: Trauma, spinal stability, and acute spinal cord injury
objectives: Describe the elements of a trauma evaluation at a conceptual level and the need for supervised multidisciplinary care.
Compare fracture morphology/stability and neurologic status as separate dimensions.
Recognize that imaging classification does not substitute for emergency assessment.
topics: cervical/thoracolumbar trauma; spinal cord injury; neurologic assessment; stability frameworks; polytrauma; timing evidence; complications
acute traumatic spinal cord injury: ISNCSCI neurologic level/AIS as standardized assessment concepts
evidence certainty and timing claims; trauma response requires an emergency multidisciplinary team
boardDomains: ACGME orthopaedic spine patient care, safety, teamwork and practice-based learning; ABNS neurosurgery primary examination
units.casePractice: Fictional blunt-trauma handoff as prose (no patient imagery): sort mechanism, neurologic observations, imaging facts, unknowns and escalation needs.
units.assessment: Build an evidence-linked trauma concept map; assess safety language, differential breadth and source date.

units.title: Spondylolisthesis, instability, and minimally invasive approaches
objectives: Explain pars-related and degenerative spondylolisthesis as distinct categories.
Discuss evidence and risks relevant to decompression/fusion decisions as population-level concepts.
Identify approach-specific exposure and complication categories without procedural steps.
topics: spondylolysis; spondylolisthesis; instability; lumbar fusion evidence; MIS concepts; lateral access anatomy and risks
degenerative and pars-related spondylolisthesis are different categories
fusion and lateral-access risk discussions as comparative concepts, never approach instruction
boardDomains: ACGME subspecialty clinical knowledge, patient safety; ABOS core orthopaedics
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional imaging descriptions for what can and cannot be inferred; avoid selecting operation.
units.assessment: One-page approach comparison graded for indication uncertainty, evidence citation and complications.

units.title: Infection, tumor, and non-degenerative spinal conditions
objectives: Develop a differential framework for infectious, neoplastic, inflammatory, and iatrogenic conditions.
Identify diagnostic urgency and multidisciplinary inputs while avoiding treatment directives.
Interpret a source describing spinal epidural infection or tumor with appropriate limitations.
topics: discitis/osteomyelitis; epidural abscess; metastasis; primary spinal tumors; biopsy principles; prior intervention; red flags
native vertebral osteomyelitis: guideline-defined suspicion, microbiology, MRI and biopsy concepts
spinal metastasis framework: neurologic, oncologic, mechanical, systemic dimensions (NOMS); distinguish framework from prescription
boardDomains: ACGME subspecialty knowledge, interprofessional practice, patient safety; ABNS core neuroscience
units.casePractice: Link to an NLM MedPix case only after inspecting its record and permissions; practice differential framing rather than definitive diagnosis.
units.assessment: Differential table with time-sensitive concerns, alternatives, evidence and explicit unknowns.

units.title: Adult spinal deformity: assessment, classification, and treatment concepts
objectives: Explain global alignment and deformity descriptors and recognize measurement variability.
Connect deformity classification with functional goals, frailty, and risk in an evidence discussion.
Critically watch an operative demonstration without interpreting it as procedural training.
topics: adult spinal deformity; sagittal/coronal balance; compensation; classification; functional outcomes; osteotomy concepts; PJK/PJF
adult spinal deformity: standing alignment, PI–LL, SVA and pelvic tilt as descriptive parameters
age/frailty, compensation, patient-reported outcomes and measurement variability; avoid universal target claims
boardDomains: ACGME orthopaedic spine educational program: disease/injury assessment and treatment; scholarship, quality and safety
units.casePractice: Review an original public lecture and a published deidentified case only by link; record goals, alternatives and outcome measures, not a real patient plan.
units.assessment: Alignment-concept sketch using fictional measurements; grade reproducibility, limits, and risk discussion.

units.title: Pediatric and congenital spine conditions
objectives: Distinguish pediatric/congenital pathology as a separate age-specific domain from adult degenerative spine.
Identify growth, development, neurologic status, and family communication as distinct considerations.
Locate a qualified pediatric spine team and current pediatric source rather than extrapolating adult studies.
topics: congenital anomalies; early-onset scoliosis; adolescent idiopathic scoliosis; growth; neuromuscular deformity; pediatric trauma
early-onset, congenital, idiopathic and neuromuscular scoliosis are age/etiology-specific domains
growth, maturity, syndrome and pulmonary considerations; no automatic adult-data extrapolation
boardDomains: ACGME fellowship scope where included in the program; not a separate pediatric spine board credential
units.casePractice: Use a public society teaching case only after checking image license; describe age-specific unknowns, never infer from adult data.
units.assessment: Age-stratified evidence note explaining limits of extrapolation.

units.title: Perioperative risk, complications, and postoperative care
objectives: Describe complication categories at a systems level and the importance of recognition, communication and supervision.
Discuss infection, neurologic deficit, dural injury, nonunion, implant failure, thromboembolism and reoperation as risks rather than predictions.
Explain why observational case volume and percent exposure do not equal independent competence.
topics: preoperative risk; optimization; positioning; blood loss; neurologic monitoring concepts; infection prevention; wound care; discharge; readmission; M&M
complication system review: neurologic, infectious, mechanical, thromboembolic and reoperation outcomes
risk adjustment and nonpunitive learning; a public exposure percentage is not competence evidence
boardDomains: ACGME competencies: patient care, medical knowledge, communication, professionalism, systems-based practice, quality improvement
units.casePractice: Fictional postoperative event review with no real records; identify timeline, safety factors, response and learning points without causal certainty.
units.assessment: Nonpunitive fictional M&M memo marked for balanced causal analysis and source-supported learning.

units.title: Complex reconstruction, osteotomies, fixation, and surgical safety
objectives: Explain at a high level the goals and risks of reconstruction/fixation options, not the execution steps.
Recognize the role of planning, anatomy, biomechanics and team capability in complex cases.
Use open operative videos as demonstrations of context only; no performance or credential is implied.
topics: pedicle screws; osteotomy categories; PSO; vertebral column resection; deformity correction; navigation/robotics as technology; neurologic/vascular risks
reconstruction/fixation/osteotomy discussions interpreted for goals and hazards only
operative demonstrations are observation-only and do not teach safe performance
boardDomains: ACGME orthopaedic spine educational program: procedural knowledge under supervision; safety, communication, professionalism
units.casePractice: Watch the public recording for anatomy/problem framing only; create a hazard analysis and state that it does not teach a safe operation.
units.assessment: Risk map scored for hazards, supervision, and explicit no-procedure boundary.

units.title: Research literacy, outcomes, quality, ethics, and board-cognitive integration
objectives: Form a focused clinical question and appraise study design, outcomes, confounding, and applicability.
Use a structured differential and explain reasoning in a short oral-format exercise.
Map knowledge to ACGME fellowship requirements and core-board status without claiming a separate spine examination.
topics: research design; registry/database limits; patient-reported outcomes; complications; QI; bias; shared decisions; handoffs; board boundaries
separate publication-level association, causal inference and evidence certainty
board boundaries and program evaluation are distinct from examination prediction or educational credit
boardDomains: ACGME scholarship/evaluation, practice-based learning, quality improvement and communication; ABOS/ABNS only their own core certifications
units.casePractice: Fictional journal-club vignette: compare one association with a causal claim and formulate a source-checked discussion.
units.assessment: 5-minute oral answer scored for problem representation, differential, evidence, uncertainty and communication; formative only.

assignment.title: Source-checked fictional spine reasoning portfolio
deliverables: A 12-unit source log recording document date, population, evidence strength and limitations.
Four fictional case analyses: lumbar degenerative finding, cervical cord compression, trauma handoff, and postoperative safety event; text only, no patient records or copied images.
A 600-word evidence update comparing one older guideline with a current source and explicitly stating uncertainty.
One short oral-style reasoning response (self-evaluated only) and a reflection distinguishing independent study from clinical training.
assignment.requirements: Use fictional educational scenarios and publicly linked sources only; do not diagnose or treat real patients, include real records/images, copy protected exam material, or rehearse/perform procedures. Cite each clinical claim and its date.
assignment.gradingBoundary: Formative independent self-study only. There is no institutional grading, human clinical review, technical skills signoff, board prediction, case credit, training credit or credential.

formativeComponents.name: Fictional case reasoning, differential and uncertainty

assessment.rubric: For each assignment score 0–4 on source accuracy, reasoning/differential, uncertainty and safety boundaries; self-study feedback only.
assessment.passingOrCertification: None. Items are original educational questions and not official ABOS/ABNS content, validated board predictors or certification tests.

studyHours.type: Transparent independent-study plan, not clinical training time
studyHours.note: Proposed study plan only. No clinical hours, rotation, call, supervision, procedural practice, patient care, case log or competency assessment included.

unitMap.text: Scope, indications, consent, and longitudinal spine evaluation
coveredTopics: spine fellowship identity; informed consent; shared decision making; functional measures; red flags; non-operative care; referral pathways
institutional variant comparison: programme page vs accreditor requirement vs certifying-board pathway
eligibility boundary and educational consent language; no independent credential or clinical privilege

unitMap.text: Spinal anatomy, biomechanics, imaging, and neurologic localization
coveredTopics: cervical/thoracic/lumbar anatomy; nerve roots; cord; sagittal/coronal balance; alignment parameters; imaging planes; degenerative findings vs symptoms
symptom–sign–imaging concordance and localization as separate inferential steps
standing full-length radiographs versus cross-sectional MRI/CT: distinct questions and limits

unitMap.text: Degenerative lumbar disease: radiculopathy, stenosis, and evidence appraisal
coveredTopics: lumbar radiculopathy; central/lateral-recess/foraminal stenosis; concordance; natural history; non-operative options; surgical evidence; complications
degenerative lumbar spondylolisthesis evidence: decompression-alone versus fusion trial synthesis
patient-reported outcomes and applicability rather than single-image thresholds

unitMap.text: Cervical spondylosis, myelopathy, and deformity
coveredTopics: degenerative cervical myelopathy; radiculopathy; cord compression; approach-selection concepts; alignment; DCM guidelines
clinical myelopathy versus nonmyelopathic cord compression; population-specific 2017 recommendations
2025 AO Spine synthesis: conditional versus strong recommendations, and MRI signal limitations

unitMap.text: Trauma, spinal stability, and acute spinal cord injury
coveredTopics: cervical/thoracolumbar trauma; spinal cord injury; neurologic assessment; stability frameworks; polytrauma; timing evidence; complications
acute traumatic spinal cord injury: ISNCSCI neurologic level/AIS as standardized assessment concepts
evidence certainty and timing claims; trauma response requires an emergency multidisciplinary team

unitMap.text: Spondylolisthesis, instability, and minimally invasive approaches
coveredTopics: spondylolysis; spondylolisthesis; instability; lumbar fusion evidence; MIS concepts; lateral access anatomy and risks
degenerative and pars-related spondylolisthesis are different categories
fusion and lateral-access risk discussions as comparative concepts, never approach instruction

unitMap.text: Infection, tumor, and non-degenerative spinal conditions
coveredTopics: discitis/osteomyelitis; epidural abscess; metastasis; primary spinal tumors; biopsy principles; prior intervention; red flags
native vertebral osteomyelitis: guideline-defined suspicion, microbiology, MRI and biopsy concepts
spinal metastasis framework: neurologic, oncologic, mechanical, systemic dimensions (NOMS); distinguish framework from prescription

unitMap.text: Adult spinal deformity: assessment, classification, and treatment concepts
coveredTopics: adult spinal deformity; sagittal/coronal balance; compensation; classification; functional outcomes; osteotomy concepts; PJK/PJF
adult spinal deformity: standing alignment, PI–LL, SVA and pelvic tilt as descriptive parameters
age/frailty, compensation, patient-reported outcomes and measurement variability; avoid universal target claims

unitMap.text: Pediatric and congenital spine conditions
coveredTopics: congenital anomalies; early-onset scoliosis; adolescent idiopathic scoliosis; growth; neuromuscular deformity; pediatric trauma
early-onset, congenital, idiopathic and neuromuscular scoliosis are age/etiology-specific domains
growth, maturity, syndrome and pulmonary considerations; no automatic adult-data extrapolation

unitMap.text: Perioperative risk, complications, and postoperative care
coveredTopics: preoperative risk; optimization; positioning; blood loss; neurologic monitoring concepts; infection prevention; wound care; discharge; readmission; M&M
complication system review: neurologic, infectious, mechanical, thromboembolic and reoperation outcomes
risk adjustment and nonpunitive learning; a public exposure percentage is not competence evidence

unitMap.text: Complex reconstruction, osteotomies, fixation, and surgical safety
coveredTopics: pedicle screws; osteotomy categories; PSO; vertebral column resection; deformity correction; navigation/robotics as technology; neurologic/vascular risks
reconstruction/fixation/osteotomy discussions interpreted for goals and hazards only
operative demonstrations are observation-only and do not teach safe performance

unitMap.text: Research literacy, outcomes, quality, ethics, and board-cognitive integration
coveredTopics: research design; registry/database limits; patient-reported outcomes; complications; QI; bias; shared decisions; handoffs; board boundaries
separate publication-level association, causal inference and evidence certainty
board boundaries and program evaluation are distinct from examination prediction or educational credit

topicGaps: The observed ready ledger now exceeds the 36-hour floor (45.490556 unique hours), but hours are concentrated in adult spinal deformity, reconstruction, alignment, and perioperative complication symposium recordings. No hour deficit remains; topic coverage is still uneven.

The new public symposium adds one trauma case discussion and pediatric/neuromuscular scoliosis coverage, but does not supply a full trauma curriculum; fracture classification, emergencies, and SCI evidence remain dependent on readings and original scripts.

Degenerative cervical myelopathy and lumbar degeneration have guideline/review readings but no newly counted full-length recordings in this expansion. Compare 2017 DCM guideline recommendations with the limited 2025 focused review; do not merge their scopes.

Infection and metastatic/primary tumor topics lack counted free recordings with verified runtimes. The IDSA 2015 NVO guideline, 2013 NOMS review, and AO tumor archive are source leads; dates and clinical applicability need review.

No complete public BIDMC or Johns Hopkins fellowship lecture series or full institutional video curriculum with observed runtimes was identified. Existing program descriptions remain separate institutional variants.

The course does not cover every adult/pediatric congenital, inflammatory, rare tumor, perioperative pathway, imaging interpretation or spine research topic in the breadth of a clinical fellowship. Original episodes are planned scripts, not rendered hours or clinical training.
remainingGaps.clinicalSkills: Supervised accredited clinical training is not supplied by these videos.

medical.boardStatus: No separate ABOS or ABNS spine fellowship board examination/certificate was identified on the official board pages checked on 2026-10-07. ABOS currently lists Hand and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine subspecialty certificates; ABNS certifies in neurological surgery. Spine fellowship is advanced clinical training, not a separate board. Confirm current rules directly with each board.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This independent course does not establish eligibility for ABOS/ABNS core specialty examinations or certification, ACGME training credit, fellowship admission, licensure, clinical competence, case credit, operative privileges, or a passing guarantee. The core orthopaedic and neurosurgical routes differ. ABNS eligibility is tied to its accredited neurosurgery residency/exam requirements; BIDMC public application requirements describe completed orthopaedic residency and ABOS board eligibility/certification. Hopkins separately describes orthopaedic or neurological surgery residency prerequisites.

officialProgrammes.institution: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center / Harvard Medical School teaching hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Spine Surgery Fellowship (Combined Spine Fellowship)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official page calls this a combined orthopaedic and neurosurgical ACGME-accredited fellowship. It reports 70% operative/30% non-operative exposure, a research/publication obligation, reading program, indications conference, M&M, Harvard combined spine journal club/lecture series and approximate exposure shares. The same page says applicants must have completed orthopaedic residency and be ABOS board-eligible or board-certified; do not infer an unlisted second neurosurgery applicant track. No public total lecture hours, individual case counts, or complete recordings catalog.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins Medicine / Johns Hopkins Hospital
officialProgrammes.name: Spine Surgery Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Distinct institutional variant. Official page states 12 months, applicants after orthopaedic or neurological surgery residency, twice-weekly conferences including didactics/case discussion/journal club/research and postoperative imaging/indications conference; reports 80% operative/20% non-operative and approximate exposures. These public proportions are not individual case logs or competence evidence.

officialProgrammes.name: Spine Surgery Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official directory-listed institutional variant; a full internal rotation or lecture curriculum was not verified in the directory discovery.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Clinical physician fellowship specialty. Preserve the actual BIDMC named fellowship variant separately from Johns Hopkins. BIDMC institutional category page redirects/links to its Orthopedics GME program page; linked page describes combined service but orthopaedic-residency application criterion. Hopkins explicitly lists both orthopaedic and neurological surgery residency applicants. Do not merge into a fictional uniform track. ACGME orthopaedic-spine requirements document is a separate source type from the institutional listing; ACGME requirement is one-year orthopaedic fellowship. Neurosurgical spine-specific board examination was not found; ABNS core neurosurgery exams apply to eligible candidates. Excludes basic science-only, non-physician spine care education, research-only posts, login-required course content, and other hospitals not in the packet.
sourceCaveats: The packet supplied a BIDMC directory/category page; the official institution’s linked programme page was fetched and describes the named combined fellowship. Its own text reports orthopaedic residency applicant prerequisites; do not infer an undocumented neurosurgery slot.
Johns Hopkins is a separate institutional variant with different applicant eligibility and publicly reported percentages. Do not merge track criteria or exposure proportions.
ACGME orthopaedic spine program requirements are not the same as institutional curriculum, board eligibility, or a specialty board examination.

No separate ABOS or ABNS spine board examination/certificate identified on official pages checked; this is bounded to the official primary pages consulted, not a claim about every independent credentialing organization.
Public exposure percentages are not case counts, individual fellow case logs, operative autonomy, or competence. No clinical outcome/diagnosis/case volume or guarantee is claimed.

Media hours count 9 unique specialty video IDs from one public playlist only. Direct playback was not independently validated; durations were observed in public playlist metadata; no media downloaded. Access can change.
No human clinical review performed; all original clips remain planned.

sourceReferences.title: ABNS Mission

sourceReferences.title: ABNS Training Requirements

sourceReferences.title: AO Spine clinical practice recommendations for DCM (2025)

sourceReferences.claimSupported: Population-specific DCM recommendations including moderate/severe and mild disease, nonmyelopathic cord compression, and radiculopathy; evidence strength varies.

sourceReferences.title: NLM MedPix

sourceReferences.title: Scoliosis Research Society — Scoliosis
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public patient education on scoliosis; background resource, not a specialty certification or independent surgical guideline.

sourceReferences.title: Spinal Deformity Symposium — Seattle Science Foundation (public playlist)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public playlist title/channel and visible recordings; exact individual runtime labels were observed for the 91 newly added unique entries on 2026-10-07. Public listing does not independently verify playback.

sourceReferences.title: IDSA Clinical Practice Guidelines for Native Vertebral Osteomyelitis in Adults
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Public guideline recommendations and strength/quality labels for suspected native vertebral osteomyelitis: clinical exam, blood cultures/ESR/CRP, MRI, biopsy indications and urgent evaluation when neurologic compromise; published guideline is 2015, not represented as a new 2026 update.

sourceReferences.title: The NOMS Framework: Approach to the Treatment of Spinal Metastatic Tumors
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Framework organizes assessment into neurologic, oncologic, mechanical and systemic dimensions; framework is a 2013 review and its specific treatment examples should not be treated as current patient-specific guidance.

sourceReferences.title: Guideline for Acute Spinal Cord Injury (2025 article in packet)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Traumatic SCI neurologic classification with ISNCSCI/AIS and early-care concepts; authors state only a minority of recommendations were evidence-based, evidence often very weak, and coverage focused on first 14 days.

sourceReferences.title: Adult spinal deformity and sagittal alignment review
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Open review describes adult kyphoscoliosis and sagittal/coronal alignment parameters while noting classification/target limitations and population variation; one regional practice review is not a universal surgical algorithm.

sourceReferences.title: Microsurgical Anatomy of Medial Temporal Lobe in North-West Indian Population: Cadaveric Brain Dissection (packet citation mismatch)
sourceReferences.claimSupported: Audit finding only: this packet URL resolves to a medial temporal lobe cadaver-dissection article and does not support spinal tumor content. Retained in source history to make the correction traceable; do not use as spine evidence.

topicGaps: The observed ready ledger now exceeds the 36-hour floor (45.490556 unique hours), but hours are concentrated in adult spinal deformity, reconstruction, alignment, and perioperative complication symposium recordings. No hour deficit remains; topic coverage is still uneven.

The new public symposium adds one trauma case discussion and pediatric/neuromuscular scoliosis coverage, but does not supply a full trauma curriculum; fracture classification, emergencies, and SCI evidence remain dependent on readings and original scripts.

Degenerative cervical myelopathy and lumbar degeneration have guideline/review readings but no newly counted full-length recordings in this expansion. Compare 2017 DCM guideline recommendations with the limited 2025 focused review; do not merge their scopes.

Infection and metastatic/primary tumor topics lack counted free recordings with verified runtimes. The IDSA 2015 NVO guideline, 2013 NOMS review, and AO tumor archive are source leads; dates and clinical applicability need review.

No complete public BIDMC or Johns Hopkins fellowship lecture series or full institutional video curriculum with observed runtimes was identified. Existing program descriptions remain separate institutional variants.

The course does not cover every adult/pediatric congenital, inflammatory, rare tumor, perioperative pathway, imaging interpretation or spine research topic in the breadth of a clinical fellowship. Original episodes are planned scripts, not rendered hours or clinical training.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public institutional page describes a combined orthopaedic/neurosurgical spine fellowship, but its application section requires an orthopaedic residency. What is the soundest scope statement?

options.text: Assume a second neurosurgery fellowship track exists
Report the page’s language and eligibility criteria as written; do not infer an undocumented separate track
Declare the title incorrect
Treat any applicant as board eligible

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official BIDMC page uses combined language but says applicants must complete orthopaedic residency and be ABOS board-eligible or certified. Preserve the discrepancy; do not invent a second neurosurgery pathway.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best distinguishes accreditation from certification?

options.text: ACGME grants specialty board certificates
ABOS accredits fellowships
ACGME accredits graduate medical education programmes; ABOS/ABNS independently certify physicians in their respective core specialties
A fellowship webpage itself grants board eligibility

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ACGME requirements are programme requirements; ABOS and ABNS are separate certifying boards. Course completion confers none of these statuses.

practiceQuestions.stem: ABOS’s official subspecialty page lists which orthopaedic subspecialty certificates?

options.text: Spine and trauma
Hand surgery and orthopaedic sports medicine
Spine and joint reconstruction
Neurosurgery and spine

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOS lists Surgery of the Hand and Orthopaedic Sports Medicine. Its page does not list a spine subspecialty certificate.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most careful statement about a separate spine-surgery board exam in the US ABMS board pathways checked here?

options.text: A separate spine-specific ABOS certificate is verified
A spine fellowship completion universally grants a new board exam
No separate spine board examination/certificate was identified on ABOS/ABNS primary board pages; orthopaedic and neurosurgical surgeons pursue their respective core board processes
NASS awards a physician license

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOS official subspecialty certificates are hand and sports medicine; ABNS describes certification in neurological surgery. No separate spine board exam was found in these primary sources; confirm directly with boards for current individual eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult has cord compression on MRI but no documented myelopathy or radiculopathy. Which summary best matches the DCM guideline?

options.text: Prophylactic surgery is recommended for all such patients
The guideline suggests not offering prophylactic surgery absent myelopathy/radiculopathy; counsel/follow as appropriate by clinicians
Imaging alone proves myelopathy
No clinical follow-up is ever relevant

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline advises against offering prophylactic surgery for nonmyelopathic patients with cord compression without radiculopathy, with counseling and clinical follow-up; this population recommendation is not patient advice.

practiceQuestions.stem: For fictional moderate or severe degenerative cervical myelopathy, what does the cited guideline recommend?

options.text: Never surgery
Recommend surgical intervention, with patient-specific care by qualified clinicians
Always observe without reassessment
Use imaging alone to determine prognosis

practiceQuestions.rationale: The guideline recommends surgery for moderate and severe DCM; evidence and individual decisions require context, and this educational item is not clinical direction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A public training page reports approximate diagnostic-category percentages for a fellowship. What may be safely inferred?

options.text: Exact case counts per trainee
Guaranteed operative competence
Only that the institution published approximate exposure proportions; not patient count or competence
That all trainees perform every operation

practiceQuestions.rationale: Percentage exposure is not a denominator of cases, individual experience, case log, operative autonomy or competence.

practiceQuestions.stem: When using a publicly viewable spinal operative video in this course, which rule is correct?

options.text: Free viewing permits downloading/rehosting
Use it as clinical authorization
Link externally, verify access, respect publisher terms and explain it is observation only
Remove the authorship label

practiceQuestions.rationale: Free-to-view does not grant redistribution or permission to teach the technique as competency. CNS/spine collection links to third-party material and some resources require login.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional MRI shows multilevel degenerative findings in a person with leg pain. What is the strongest board-cognitive next step?

options.text: Assume the most dramatic image finding is causal
Check symptom, examination and imaging concordance and preserve alternative diagnoses
Diagnose without history
Promise a specific outcome

practiceQuestions.rationale: Degenerative imaging findings require clinical correlation; a careful problem representation and differential avoids unsupported certainty.

practiceQuestions.stem: What is a valid interpretation of this independent course’s final assessment score?

options.text: Evidence of board eligibility
A validated estimate of passing ABOS/ABNS
Formative self-study feedback only; no clinical or certification meaning
An operative privileges credential

practiceQuestions.rationale: No clinical review, affiliation, accreditation, supervised training or validation is supplied. Scores are not board predictors or credentialing evidence.

title: Surgical Critical Care Fellowship
level: Clinical physician fellowship (with an institutional pediatric/health-outcomes research combined variant)-aligned independent study
prerequisites: For physician learners: completed medical school and substantial postgraduate general surgery training; prior general surgery completion is the usual fellow level described by Hopkins. BCH notes three years of general surgical training before entry in its programme description. These are programme descriptions, not a universal eligibility ruling.
Advanced understanding of physiology, pathology, pharmacology, infectious disease, trauma, perioperative care and evidence appraisal.
For other learners: educational reading only, not a credential or a patient-care scope expansion. Adult and pediatric critical care content is not interchangeable.
objectives: Map published ABS SCC examination categories and care dimensions to a deliberate study plan without implying the blueprint is a full syllabus.

Explain mechanisms and evidence for common surgical ICU problems across cardiovascular, respiratory, renal, neurologic, endocrine, nutritional, infectious, hematologic, gastrointestinal, trauma, burn, pediatric, transplant, pharmacologic, monitoring, administration, ethical and legal domains.
Apply safe clinical reasoning to fictional de-identified cases: differential, tests, monitoring, treatment evidence, indications/limits, complications and outcome considerations.
Distinguish official institutional programme description, ACGME accreditation requirements, ABS certification requirements and independent course content.
Critically appraise evidence and state uncertainty, high-risk modifiers, need for supervised clinical judgment and local protocols.

mapping.institution: Boston Children’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School teaching hospital)
mapping.name: Surgical Critical Care Fellowship — pediatric-focused ACGME-approved fellowship with outcomes-research year
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official BCH page describes three two-year positions: initial 12-month pediatric ICU clinical rotation (NICU and medical/surgical ICU, in conjunction with pediatric surgery and ICU teams), then 12 months outcomes research in pediatric surgical disciplines, with option to extend research by 24 months. The page says ACGME-approved, an ABS ACQ route, and candidates have completed three years general-surgery training to be “board eligible.” This is a combined clinical/research emphasis, not a research-only non-physician job; research time is not clinical fellowship time. Distinct from Hopkins adult track.

mapping.name: Surgical Critical Care/Acute Care Surgery Fellowship — one-year ACGME SCC + separate second-year AAST-approved ACS component

The Year 2 is not treated as SCC certification training.

mapping.institution: Brigham and Women’s Hospital (Harvard Medical School-affiliated)
mapping.name: Surgical Critical Care Fellowship — one-year ACGME physician fellowship; optional second-year non-ACGME acute care surgery and global-surgery emphasis

medical.trackType: Clinical physician fellowship (with an institutional pediatric/health-outcomes research combined variant)
boardNames: American Board of Surgery (ABS) — Surgical Critical Care Certifying Examination (SCC CE)
medical.boardStatus: ABS offers a separate surgical critical care subspecialty certificate/ACQ through the annual SCC CE. ABS describes this as its single SCC exam required for board certification; primary ABS surgery certification (or other specified pathway), accredited clinical training, 48 weeks full-time clinical activity, case-report, license and other requirements still apply. ACGME accreditation is a programme status, not board certification. Not a separate pediatric surgical-critical-care board exam identified for the BCH variant; it is a pediatric-focused route to the ABS SCC qualification. Neurocritical care is a distinct adjacent subspecialty and is not silently merged into this programme.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: This self-study curriculum confers no board eligibility. ABS eligibility is determined only by the current ABS requirements; course hours, quiz scores, simulated cases or completion do not satisfy fellowship, operative/case-log, primary certification, license, privileges or other requirements. ABS rules are date-sensitive; candidates must verify at application time.

Distinct from Hopkins adult track.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Supplied packet named Johns Hopkins and Boston Children’s. Additional official Harvard-affiliated searches verified MGH, BWH and BIDMC; all are preserved as distinct institutional variants. Hopkins/BWH/BIDMC describe one-year ACGME SCC; MGH describes ACGME SCC Year 1 with AAST-approved ACS Year 2; BCH describes pediatric clinical SCC Year 1 and outcomes research Year 2. This is a clinical physician specialty, not a generic directory category or research-only job. MGH/BWH ACS extensions and BCH research time are distinguished from SCC training. No separate pediatric SCC board exam identified. Current program availability and board/accreditation rules can change.

topicGaps: 36-hour verified recording floor remains short by 32.4944 hours: 5 newly verified Society of Mechanical Ventilation recordings total 12620 seconds (3.5056 h). Scripted minutes are not rendered/accessible video hours.

Five added public recordings are concentrated in respiratory/ventilator physiology, ECMO concepts and pediatric ventilation; the other blueprint categories (initial resuscitation, cardiovascular, renal/electrolyte, neurologic, endocrine/nutrition, infection, hematology/transfusion, GI/GU/OB-GYN, trauma/burn, transplant, pharmacology, systems, ethics) still lack a verified full-length freely playable recording sequence in this audit.

Pre-existing candidate links remain uncounted where no-login playback was not independently confirmed; 16 now have a playlist-displayed runtime but still require individual access verification, while other entries have unknown runtime.

No complete public didactic calendar was found for the listed institutional variants. Boston Children’s pediatric clinical year is distinct from its research year and from adult SCC case mix; pediatric/neonatal equivalence is not claimed.

No qualified human clinician review was performed. Current local protocols, board requirements, guidelines, drug/device labels and patient-specific clinical judgment supersede this educational self-study.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional postoperative adult has possible infection and new organ dysfunction. Which principle best matches the 2026 adult SSC guideline?

options.text: Sepsis can be confirmed or excluded by one biomarker.
Use qSOFA alone as the preferred hospital screening tool.
Sepsis is a clinical diagnosis; no single biomarker/test rules it in or out.
Wait for culture results before considering the diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 SSC states sepsis is a clinical diagnosis and should not be ruled in or out using one biomarker or test. Screening tool recommendations are separate from diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinically unstable patient is being evaluated for suspected sepsis. Which guideline-consistent statement about cultures is most accurate?

options.text: Obtain blood cultures as soon as possible, ideally before antimicrobials, without delaying emergency care.
Cultures are unnecessary if lactate is elevated.
Wait until antimicrobial therapy is complete.
A negative culture excludes sepsis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: 2026 SSC recommends blood cultures as soon as possible and ideally before antimicrobial therapy; sepsis remains a clinical diagnosis.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the most accurate summary of the 2026 SSC initial-fluid statement for adults with sepsis-induced hypoperfusion or septic shock?

options.text: A fixed volume is mandatory for every adult regardless of context.
Suggest at least 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid in first 3 hours, with individual context and repeated reassessment.
Fluids should never be used in septic shock.
Do not reassess after an initial bolus.

practiceQuestions.rationale: This is a conditional suggestion with low certainty and explicit remarks to consider individual characteristics and reassess often for under- or over-resuscitation; not a universal order.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees an ICP value just above 22 mm Hg in severe TBI. Which statement accurately reflects the BTF guideline page?

options.text: An ICP above 22 mm Hg is a Level II B treatment threshold recommendation, interpreted with the clinical context.
Every ICP above 15 requires immediate surgery.
Hyperosmolar agent superiority is conclusively established.
Steroids improve survival.

practiceQuestions.rationale: BTF lists treating ICP above 22 mm Hg as Level II B; thresholds are interpreted with clinical and imaging findings. The guideline states insufficient evidence to favor a specific hyperosmolar agent; steroids are not recommended for outcome/ICP and high-dose methylprednisolone is contraindicated.

practiceQuestions.stem: A severe-TBI lecture claims prophylactic hypothermia reliably improves outcome. What is the evidence-aligned response from the BTF 4th edition?

options.text: Accept; Level I recommendation.
Reject as a proven benefit: early short-term prophylactic hypothermia is not recommended to improve outcome in diffuse injury.
Use hypothermia in all trauma.
Guideline gives no statement on this topic.

practiceQuestions.rationale: BTF states early (within 2.5 hours), short-term (48 hours) prophylactic hypothermia is not recommended to improve outcomes in diffuse injury; this is not a treatment prescription for an individual.

practiceQuestions.stem: A trauma patient has hemorrhage risk and an abnormal coagulation profile. What is the safest educational reasoning step?

options.text: Rely on one laboratory value as a complete measure of hemostasis.
Integrate bleeding context, serial assessment and relevant coagulation tests; follow local transfusion protocol and senior team direction.
Apply an identical component ratio to every patient regardless of context.
Ignore transfusion complications.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ACGME includes assessment of coagulation and appropriate component therapy; ABS blueprint tests diagnosis, monitoring, treatment and complications. This item tests reasoning/safety, not a specific transfusion protocol.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement best characterizes Johns Hopkins and Boston Children’s offerings?

options.text: They are the same identical curriculum and adult case mix.
Hopkins lists a one-year ACGME-accredited SCC fellowship; BCH describes a pediatric-focused clinical year plus outcomes-research year, both linked to ABS SCC qualification.
BCH research year replaces ABS board certification.
The BCH track is a research-only non-physician job.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The official Hopkins page describes a one-year ACGME program; BCH describes an ACGME-approved fellowship with 12 months pediatric ICU clinical care and an outcomes research second year/option to extend. Preserve these variants; research is not the same as a board examination.

practiceQuestions.stem: What examination does ABS identify as required for board certification in surgical critical care?

options.text: A separate ACGME exam.
The annual Surgical Critical Care Certifying Examination; primary certification and other requirements also matter.
The general surgery QE alone.
No examination exists.

practiceQuestions.stem: A critically ill patient has a rising lactate. Which interpretation is most defensible?

options.text: Lactate alone proves bacterial sepsis.
Lactate is a contextual marker; review perfusion, trend and alternative causes.
A normal lactate excludes sepsis.
Lactate eliminates the need to reassess.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2026 SSC recommends measuring lactate in possible/probable/definite sepsis or septic shock, but explicitly warns that a single biomarker/test should not rule sepsis in or out.

Remove attribution to protect patient privacy.
Assume every case has identical independent licensing.

mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The exact official directory item labels this ACGME-accredited, three years, at Johns Hopkins Bayview. Department page calls it ACGME-accredited, says clinical training spans Johns Hopkins Bayview and Greater Baltimore Medical Center, lists vaginal, abdominal, laparoscopic and robotic surgery, office procedures, neuromodulation and complex urodynamics, multidisciplinary pelvic health and optional global-health experience. Its stated entry requirement is ACGME-accredited OB/GYN residency and Maryland medical-licensure eligibility. The three-year program is the Hopkins institution variant; do not infer a 24-month urology route from this page. It is a clinical physician fellowship, not a generic directory-only category.

unitMap.text: Pelvic-floor anatomy, physiology and vocabulary
coveredTopics: Pelvic support and innervation; pelvic organ and anorectal function; terminology; conceptual pelvic floor models.

unitMap.text: History, examination, symptom burden and POP-Q
coveredTopics: Symptom scales and bother; pelvic examination; POP-Q; red flags and alternate pelvic pathology; documentation.

unitMap.text: Female urinary incontinence phenotypes and differential
coveredTopics: Bladder diary, urinalysis/PVR context, comorbid contributors, urinary symptoms after prior surgery, hematuria and infection clues.

unitMap.text: Urodynamics, imaging and diagnostic reasoning
coveredTopics: Stress leak demonstration; bladder emptying; urodynamic uncertainty; selective cystoscopy/imaging; pelvic-floor ultrasound/MRI as adjuncts.

unitMap.text: Pelvic organ prolapse: conservative care and pessary management
coveredTopics: Observation; pelvic-floor muscle training; pessary choice/fitting/care; topical vaginal estrogen context; prolapse symptoms vs exam.

unitMap.text: Stress urinary incontinence and continence procedures: decision framework
coveredTopics: PFMT, pessary, observation; retropubic/transobturator/single-incision sling, autologous fascial sling, Burch and bulking; index vs non-index context.

unitMap.text: Overactive bladder, voiding dysfunction and advanced therapies
coveredTopics: OAB as a clinical syndrome; bladder training; beta-3 agonist/antimuscarinic considerations; PTNS, sacral neuromodulation, intradetrusor botulinum toxin; incomplete emptying.

unitMap.text: Prolapse reconstructive options, apical support and outcomes
coveredTopics: Vaginal, abdominal/laparoscopic/robotic approaches; native tissue, mesh/graft and uterine-preservation discussions; sexual function, recurrence and patient-reported outcomes.

unitMap.text: Postoperative complications, mesh concerns and lower urinary tract injury
coveredTopics: Voiding dysfunction, exposure/erosion, pain, infection, recurrent symptoms; bladder/ureter injury recognition themes; urinary tract fistula differential.

unitMap.text: Bowel dysfunction, fecal incontinence and pelvic-floor fistulas
coveredTopics: Anorectal physiology; stool consistency; symptom scales; imaging and anorectal testing in context; rectovaginal fistula differential and team collaboration.

unitMap.text: Pelvic-floor pain, sexual function, life course and equitable care
coveredTopics: Pelvic pain and dyspareunia; pregnancy after pelvic-floor treatment; aging, menopause, access barriers and shared decision-making.

unitMap.text: Evidence appraisal, research ethics, quality and educational practice
coveredTopics: Clinical trial literacy; outcomes and patient-reported measures; quality improvement vs research; consent/privacy; scholarly activity and teaching.

topicGaps: The 36-hour verified-video floor remains unmet: 17 unique, accessible, full-length recordings total 59,824 observed seconds (16.6178 hours); the residual gap is 19.3822 hours. Planned scripts and targetMinutes do not count as media or verified hours.

Long-form coverage is still sparse for pelvic-floor neuroanatomy and physiology; symptom scales, epidemiology and research methods; examination/POP-Q reasoning; conservative care and pessary management; prolapse outcomes and current surgical evidence; and equitable, life-course and sexual-function care.

The added specialist recordings broaden coverage of pelvic-floor ultrasound, neuro-urology, SUI surgery, graft science, fecal incontinence, infection and postoperative pain, but they are educational talks from 2020–2024 rather than a comprehensive or current course. Check the guidance in force for every dated recommendation.

ABU's detailed exam-content PDF was not fully extractable and ABOG's eligibility detail remained dynamically unavailable in the source packet. Exact board-domain weights are not asserted; current board requirements and the distinction between ABOG and ABU routes still require direct verification.

medical.trackType: Clinical physician subspecialty fellowship (institution-specific OB/GYN and urology entry tracks distinguished; Hopkins page describes OB/GYN origin)
boardNames: American Board of Obstetrics and Gynecology (ABOG) — Urogynecology and Reconstructive Pelvic Surgery (URPS) subspecialty certification route for eligible OB/GYN diplomates; ABOG’s public site describes subspecialty qualifying and certifying steps. Hopkins identifies ABOG certification. Current eligibility and steps must be confirmed in current ABOG policies; the dynamic detailed eligibility pages did not expose the underlying policy text in this check.

American Board of Urology (ABU) — URPS subspecialty certification, a separate board pathway/examination for eligible urologists. ABU currently describes approved applicants with current unrestricted general urology certification, an ACGME-accredited URPS fellowship of at least 24 months, active URPS practice and case-log/CME/licensure requirements; annual exam. This is not the Johns Hopkins OB/GYN track.
medical.boardStatus: This is an actual physician subspecialty/fellowship rather than a directory category, research-only postdoctoral job, or non-physician supplement. ABOG and ABU renamed their jointly sponsored Female Pelvic Medicine and Reconstructive Surgery (FPMRS) subspecialty to Urogynecology and Reconstructive Pelvic Surgery (URPS), effective 2024-01-01. A distinct URPS subspecialty certification/examination exists for the ABU urology route; ABU states the examination is annual. ABOG likewise maintains a URPS subspecialty certification process with qualifying/certifying steps, although its detailed eligibility page returned only dynamic loading placeholders in this check. ABU expressly directs candidates from ABOG-sponsored residency programmes to ABOG. The 2026 ABU exam date on the page (2026-07-20) had passed at check date 2026-10-07; verify 2027 dates/requirements. Do not treat board exams as one unified test or claim eligibility from course completion.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Educational self-study only. Does not grant affiliation with Johns Hopkins, Harvard, MGH, BIDMC, Mount Auburn, AUGS, ACGME, ABOG or ABU; accredited graduate medical education; medical licensure; board eligibility or certification; procedure competence; operative experience/case counts; independent clinical authority; or exam success. officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Bayview Medical Center
officialProgrammes.name: Urogynecology and Reconstructive Pelvic Surgery Fellowship (Obstetrics & Gynecology-origin track)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The exact official directory item labels this ACGME-accredited, three years, at Johns Hopkins Bayview. Department page calls it ACGME-accredited, says clinical training spans Johns Hopkins Bayview and Greater Baltimore Medical Center, lists vaginal, abdominal, laparoscopic and robotic surgery, office procedures, neuromodulation and complex urodynamics, multidisciplinary pelvic health and optional global-health experience. Its stated entry requirement is ACGME-accredited OB/GYN residency and Maryland medical-licensure eligibility. The three-year program is the Hopkins institution variant; do not infer a 24-month urology route from this page. It is a clinical physician fellowship, not a generic directory-only category.

officialProgrammes.institution: Massachusetts General Hospital / Harvard Medical School-affiliated, Mass General Brigham
officialProgrammes.name: MGH Urogynecology and Reconstructive Pelvic Surgery Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official MGH page calls the fellowship ACGME-accredited and established 2012, accepts applicants from OB/GYN and urology pathways, and publicly describes one year dedicated research plus two years clinical. Public curriculum includes weekly didactics, journal/case conferences, M&M, interdisciplinary pelvic-floor conference, four clinical sites, clinics, urodynamics, ultrasound and selected office procedures. It says ERAS and AUGS/NRMP match. The institution describes high surgical volumes; no volume figure is imported into this self-study curriculum or treated as guaranteed trainee access.

officialProgrammes.institution: Beth Israel Deaconess Medical Center (BIDMC), Harvard Medical School Teaching Hospital; Mount Auburn Hospital (clinical rotation site)
officialProgrammes.name: Urogynecology and Reconstructive Pelvic Surgery Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official BIDMC page identifies a physician clinical fellowship based in its OB/GYN department with rotations available at Mount Auburn Hospital. It describes weekly didactics, surgery/clinic, laparoscopy emphasis, integrated colorectal/urology/gastroenterology opportunities, research methods, and resident/fellow teaching. The BIDMC page did not state ACGME status, total fellowship duration, or a board pathway during this check; do not claim these without ACGME/board confirmation. Mount Auburn is listed as a clinical partner/site, not as a separately verified fellowship variant.

medical.programmeSourceScope: Exact item packet named the Johns Hopkins Medicine fellowship. It is confirmed as a three-year ACGME-accredited clinical fellowship. Cross-check of official Harvard-affiliated pages found MGH’s ACGME-accredited URPS fellowship and BIDMC’s clinical fellowship page. These are separate institutional variants, not one merged programme; Mount Auburn is a BIDMC clinical rotation site, not independently counted. Hopkins clinical training at Bayview/GBMC and its optional global health rotation are experiences in one Hopkins program, not combined fellowships. MGH accepts both OB/GYN and urology applicants and describes one research and two clinical years; an ACGME FAQ distinguishes 24- and 36-month pathways based on prior residency, so actual track length/board eligibility must be confirmed per programme and board. BIDMC page did not state accreditation status or duration. No research-only postdoctoral role or non-physician training course is counted as a residency/fellowship variant. Physical therapy, colorectal and urology collaboration are interprofessional clinical experiences, not a non-physician certification track.
sourceCaveats: Programme pages document official named programmes, but do not guarantee current availability, accreditation at every location, trainee exposure or case numbers. Reconfirm with ACGME and each institution.
The ACGME FAQ is explicitly effective July 1, 2020; current ACGME program requirements control.
ABOG subspecialty eligibility pages were dynamic and displayed loading placeholders in stateless extraction; eligibility details were not independently verified.

ABU’s public page states 2026 exam date July 20, which had passed by check date; verify later dates and current handbook. The official content PDF returned a security/cookie interstitial, so no precise board-domain weights are asserted.

AUGS guidance page includes some linked journal content that is member/subscriber restricted; no bypass. ACOG full bulletin is subscription/member restricted, although abstract and figure description are public.

AUGS webinar series is listed as fully viewable on its YouTube channel; individual pages were checked for open playback and runtime. Free viewing conveys no republication, extraction, derivative or embedding rights.
No cases, images, patient records, surgical footage or proprietary exam questions have been copied. All generated vignettes/questions are fictional.
Clinical sources are date sensitive. Check newer AUA/SUFU, AUGS, ACOG, NICE, FDA and board guidance before use. The course is not clinical advice and has no human clinical review.
