practiceQuestions.stem: A patient has bothersome urgency and frequency without a neurologic disorder. Which statement best reflects the AUA/SUFU idiopathic OAB guideline?

options.text: Urodynamic detrusor overactivity must be demonstrated before OAB can be diagnosed.
OAB is a clinical syndrome; urodynamics may be considered when response is inadequate or diagnosis remains uncertain.
Cystoscopy is required to establish uncomplicated OAB.
Any patient with urgency should proceed directly to surgery.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AUA/SUFU guideline identifies OAB as a clinical diagnosis; urodynamics are not required but may help when symptoms are atypical or treatment response is inadequate. Detrusor overactivity is neither required nor by itself diagnostic.

practiceQuestions.stem: A clinician is considering intradetrusor botulinum toxin for a patient with OAB. What baseline safety check is explicitly recommended by the AUA/SUFU guideline?

options.text: Routine pelvic MRI.
Measure post-void residual before injection.
Routine cystoscopy for every OAB patient.
No assessment is needed if the patient has urgency.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The 2024 AUA/SUFU guideline says clinicians should measure PVR before intradetrusor botulinum toxin and obtain it again if symptoms fail to improve or worsen afterward. This question tests guideline recall, not procedural competence.

practiceQuestions.stem: A specialist is documenting a patient referred for prolapse. Which exam documentation aligns with NICE NG123?

options.text: Record only whether the patient reports a bulge.
Document anterior, central and posterior compartment prolapse with POP-Q and assess pelvic-floor muscle activity, tissue and alternate pathology.
Obtain MRI routinely even if examination already documents prolapse.
Use imaging to determine patient preference.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE recommends specialist assessment of degree in the anterior, central and posterior compartments using POP-Q, pelvic-floor activity, tissue change and possible alternative pathology. It advises against routine imaging solely to document a prolapse found on examination.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: a patient with symptomatic POP-Q stage 1 or 2 asks about nonoperative choices. Which option is supported in NICE NG123?

options.text: Supervised pelvic-floor muscle training for at least 16 weeks may be considered as a first option.
Immediate surgery is mandatory.
No treatment discussion is needed.
Routine pelvic imaging is necessary before any conservative care.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NICE NG123 recommends considering supervised pelvic-floor muscle training for at least 16 weeks as a first option for symptomatic stage 1 or 2 prolapse, with continuation if beneficial. Options remain individualized and local guidance may differ.

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with stress-predominant mixed urinary incontinence asks about surgery. Which is a required counseling point before selecting a midurethral synthetic sling under the AUA/SUFU SUI guideline?

options.text: Discuss mesh-specific risks and benefits and alternatives to a mesh sling.
Tell the patient that a sling is the only effective treatment.
Avoid discussing complications because the device is FDA cleared.
Promise cure based on a positive stress test.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AUA/SUFU guideline makes informed counseling on the specific risks and benefits of mesh and alternatives a clinical principle before synthetic sling selection. Treatment options should be individualized and no cure is guaranteed.

practiceQuestions.stem: In an otherwise uncomplicated, clearly demonstrated index-patient SUI case, which testing statement is consistent with AUA/SUFU guidance?

options.text: Cystoscopy is routinely required in every index patient.
Urodynamics may be omitted when SUI is clearly demonstrated; additional evaluation may be considered for non-index features.
Urodynamics must always demonstrate detrusor overactivity.
Cystoscopy replaces symptom assessment.

practiceQuestions.rationale: AUA/SUFU says clinicians may omit urodynamics in a clearly demonstrated index patient seeking treatment and should not perform cystoscopy in index patients unless concern for urinary tract abnormality exists; non-index contexts can prompt additional evaluation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement correctly distinguishes the ABU URPS route from the Johns Hopkins institutional fellowship page?

options.text: All graduates of the Hopkins fellowship automatically receive ABU certification.
ABU describes a separate urology subspecialty certification exam and eligibility requirements; Hopkins publicly describes a three-year ACGME-accredited fellowship and requires OB/GYN residency.
URPS has no board examination.
A self-study course may substitute for an ACGME-accredited fellowship.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABU route is distinct and includes an annual exam and required criteria; Hopkins identifies its own 3-year ACGME programme and OB/GYN residency requirement. Course participation confers none of these.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is accurate about the current subspecialty name?

options.text: FPMRS changed to URPS in 2024 under the joint ABOG/ABU announcement.
URPS was only a research category and not a physician subspecialty.
The name change abolished subspecialty certification.
The change made the ABOG and ABU pathways identical.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABOG and ABU announced the jointly sponsored subspecialty name change effective January 1, 2024. The change does not merge distinct board pathways or remove eligibility requirements.

practiceQuestions.stem: Fictional case: a person reports vaginal bulge but exam findings do not explain the symptom. Which next conceptual approach is supported by NICE NG123?

options.text: Assume the symptom is not real.
Consider repeating examination with standing or squatting, or at a different time, and reconsider the differential.
Use one POP-Q point as an automatic surgery threshold.

medical.programmeSourceScope: One exact institution variant is present in packet. Verified public listings show an institutional category title and the detailed Epstein minimally invasive urologic surgery fellowship; this is a clinical post-urology-residency physician training program according to the program description. It is not merely a generic category, combined residency/fellowship or research-only postdoctoral role. It is distinct as an institutional training track, not a separately named ABU specialty exam. BIDMC page attributes program accreditation to the Endourology Society. Do not conflate this with SUO urologic oncology fellowship accreditation. A nearby BIDMC Urologic Oncology Research Fellowship is research-only and is not this program.
sourceCaveats: The detailed BIDMC program page states Endourology Society accreditation; it does not establish SUO accreditation or ABU board certification.

BIDMC public program description does not publish full rotations, a detailed didactic syllabus, current admissions/eligibility requirements, or fellow-specific case logs. Do not infer individual case volume from annual program-wide exposure.

ABU official certification page describes general urology qualifying/certifying exams. Its 2025 URPS handbook describes Pediatric Urology and URPS subspecialty categories; neither is this minimally invasive urologic cancer track.
SUO requirements and OKAT apply to SUO-accredited oncology fellowship programs; use them only as a curricular-domain comparator, not as BIDMC program facts.
IU publicly advertises recorded lectures, but linked Kaltura collections redirected to SSO, so media-level runtimes and free public access could not be confirmed.

The verified recordings cover bladder staging/pathology and kidney/UTUC/kidney-health context. Their community-facing format and substantial Q&A limit suitability as advanced clinical fellowship teaching.

No qualifying runtimes were found for prostate MRI/biopsy and robotic prostatectomy, kidney minimally invasive procedure technique, cystectomy/diversion operative phases, systemic therapy decision algorithms, simulation/credentialing, or comprehensive clinical effectiveness methods. These remain source-grounded original-production or future verified-recording needs.
The previously recorded Indiana University Kaltura candidates remain unknown/unverified because linked playlists redirect to institutional SSO; they are not counted.

A complete 36-hour free, public, runtime-verified specialty-level recording set was not established. Original scripts are pedagogical supplements, not video hours; residual feasibility remains dependent on future recording discovery and production.
medical.sourceReviewNote: Source-cited research and automated checks; not clinician validation or exam-passing prediction.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional localized prostate-cancer case is being discussed. Which is the best way to frame the treatment conference?

options.text: Treat the MRI score alone as the final diagnosis and select surgery.
Integrate pathology, stage/risk, patient factors and preferences; compare appropriate options and multidisciplinary input.
All localized disease requires prostatectomy.
Ignore risk group because all cases have identical prognosis.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ describes stage-dependent treatment options; a conference should integrate tumor data, health status, options and preferences rather than make a modality automatic.

practiceQuestions.stem: A renal mass discussion lacks information on renal function, contralateral kidney and detailed imaging. What is the strongest next educational response?

options.text: Assume partial nephrectomy is always preferred.
Assume radical nephrectomy is always preferred.
Identify missing characterization and functional data before comparing options.
Use PI-RADS to assign renal mass risk.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The choice among options depends on tumor and patient factors; missing data must be identified. PI-RADS is a prostate system and is not a renal classification.

practiceQuestions.stem: A bladder resection pathology report does not state whether muscularis propria is present. Why is that an important limitation?

options.text: It prevents reliable discussion of whether muscle invasion was assessed in the specimen.
It proves metastatic disease.
It proves low-grade disease.
It establishes a prostate primary.

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ notes the role of muscularis propria in determining whether tumor invades bladder muscle; missing muscle can leave staging uncertain.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional bladder tumor is reported as muscle-invasive. Which broad planning principle best fits the NCI PDQ framework?

options.text: Discuss stage-appropriate multidisciplinary options; do not assume one surgery is suitable for everyone.
Use intravesical treatment alone in every case.
No systemic therapy can be relevant.
Do not consider patient goals.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Stage II/III bladder-cancer treatment options include cystectomy-based and bladder-preserving pathways and perioperative systemic therapy considerations; specific management is individualized.

practiceQuestions.stem: The public BIDMC fellowship page calls the fellowship accredited by which body?

options.text: ACGME, as a robotic oncology subspecialty.
Endourology Society.
ABU board certification.
SUO, according to the public page.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The BIDMC program page states Endourology Society accreditation. It does not say that the fellowship is an ACGME fellowship or that it confers ABU certification or SUO accreditation.

practiceQuestions.stem: Which ABU statement is appropriate for this course?

options.text: Completing this online curriculum qualifies a learner for ABU certification.
ABU certification is a separate pathway with required training and qualifying/certifying examinations; the course grants neither eligibility nor certification.
The BIDMC fellowship itself is the ABU board exam.
All fellowships have a board examination.

practiceQuestions.rationale: ABU describes its urology certification examination pathway; its official handbook lists subspecialty credentials in Pediatric Urology and URPS, not minimally invasive cancer surgery. The course grants no eligibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner watches a robotic operation video and finishes an online quiz. What can the learner legitimately conclude?

options.text: They are competent and may independently operate.
They have completed a limited educational activity; competence, supervised training, credentialing and privileges are separate.
They satisfy all hospital credentialing rules.
They have completed a clinical fellowship.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Self-study does not demonstrate operative competence. Institutions grant privileges based on their own credentialing and supervised-training requirements; this online curriculum is not sign-off.

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner accesses a TCIA image dataset for a case exercise. Which practice is correct?

options.text: Try to match the de-identified images to public individuals to infer missing details.
Cite the dataset, comply with its license and usage policy, and do not attempt participant identification.
Copy all images into a course pack without checking license.
Treat the research images as a real-time patient-care record.

practiceQuestions.rationale: TCIA requires dataset citation and prohibits identification attempts; the page-level license and repository use restrictions apply.

practiceQuestions.stem: A renal-cancer paper reports a treatment effect in a metastatic cohort. What is the soundest interpretation for a localized renal-mass discussion?

options.text: Apply the result directly without checking population or comparator.
Check eligibility, disease setting, comparator, endpoints and applicability before extrapolating.
Assume every endpoint is overall survival.
Treat an association as proof of causation.

practiceQuestions.rationale: Evidence appraisal requires matching population and setting and interpreting endpoints and design. NCI PDQ summarizes disease-stage-specific treatment evidence; one setting should not be casually generalized to another.

practiceQuestions.stem: A course creator sees several hundred laparoscopic and robotic cases per year listed for a program. What can be inferred about an individual fellow’s exposure?

options.text: Every fellow personally performs several hundred cases.
It proves competence in every listed procedure.
Only that the public description reports overall program exposure; individual fellow logs and competence are not established.
It guarantees ABU board passage.

practiceQuestions.rationale: The BIDMC page reports overall program exposure and does not provide individual fellow case logs or guarantee competence, certification, or examination outcomes.

practiceQuestions.stem: A 63-year-old with fever, rigors, hypotension and a ureteral calculus causing hydronephrosis has urine studies consistent with infection. Which immediate principle is most appropriate?

options.text: Give oral fluids and observe for stone passage
Start immediate antimicrobial therapy and urgently decompress the collecting system; defer definitive stone removal until infection resolves
Proceed directly to elective ureteroscopy without drainage
Treat pain alone and repeat imaging in a week
Perform nephrectomy as routine first step

practiceQuestions.rationale: Infection with an obstructed collecting system is an emergency. Obtain cultures, start antibiotics promptly and urgently drain by ureteral stent or nephrostomy; delay definitive stone removal until sepsis resolves. The specific method depends on context/resources, not a single universally preferred technique.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABU core domain; source mapping as cited

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient with renal colic is stable, afebrile, has preserved renal function and a small distal ureteral stone. Which assessment should guide conservative management versus intervention?

options.text: Stone size/location, symptoms, infection/obstruction risk, renal function, patient context and follow-up reliability
Urinalysis alone, regardless of symptoms
Serum calcium only
Prostate-specific antigen
A fixed universal time threshold independent of context

practiceQuestions.rationale: Stone location/size and clinical context including infection, renal function, symptom control and follow-up inform management. Uncomplicated passage may be considered; deterioration or refractory symptoms change urgency.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABU core domain; source mapping as cited

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about gross hematuria is most defensible?

options.text: It is benign if painless
It warrants a structured evaluation based on risk and clinical context; infection does not automatically exclude other causes
It proves bladder cancer
A normal dipstick makes evaluation unnecessary
It is always caused by stones

practiceQuestions.rationale: Hematuria has a broad differential including malignancy, stone, infection, renal disease and trauma. Risk-appropriate evaluation matters; an identified infection does not automatically rule out coexisting pathology.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABU core domain; source mapping as cited

practiceQuestions.stem: A man with bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms asks whether a larger prostate necessarily proves outlet obstruction. Best response?

options.text: Yes, prostate volume alone diagnoses obstruction
No; symptoms, examination, residual/flow and selected tests are interpreted together; size and symptom burden do not perfectly map to obstruction
No tests are ever useful
PSA establishes obstruction
Cystoscopy is mandatory for every patient

practiceQuestions.rationale: Prostate size, symptoms and physiologic obstruction are related imperfectly. Evaluate differential causes and use testing selectively; goals and adverse effects matter in management.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABU core domain; source mapping as cited

practiceQuestions.stem: A hypothetical prostate biopsy confirms localized adenocarcinoma. Which approach best supports treatment selection?

options.text: Choose prostatectomy for everyone
Integrate risk group, stage, health/life expectancy, preferences, and trade-offs among surveillance, surgery and radiotherapy
Select therapy from PSA alone
Use metastatic treatment regardless of stage
Ignore pathology grade

practiceQuestions.rationale: Treatment is stage/risk-dependent and preference-sensitive; the NCI PDQ describes options across disease states and highlights that clinical context affects choice.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABU core domain; source mapping as cited

practiceQuestions.stem: A bladder tumor is classified as Ta/Tis/T1 on initial resection. Which distinction is central to subsequent management planning?

options.text: Non-muscle-invasive tumors are risk-stratified and followed with resection/intravesical/surveillance pathways as appropriate; muscle-invasive disease requires different staging and treatment discussion
Ta means metastatic disease
All NMIBC requires immediate cystectomy
Histology is irrelevant
All tumors receive identical therapy

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ notes NMIBC care is risk-based following transurethral resection, whereas MIBC treatment has distinct curative pathways including cisplatin-based neoadjuvant treatment plus cystectomy or chemoradiation in selected settings. Individual current guidelines should govern.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABU core domain; source mapping as cited

practiceQuestions.stem: A patient presents with a painless testicular mass suspicious for a germ-cell tumor. Which is a useful initial conceptual workup component?

options.text: Serum AFP, beta-hCG and LDH alongside imaging and prompt specialist evaluation
PSA only
Urine cytology only
Delay assessment until pain develops
A single marker that excludes all germ-cell tumors

practiceQuestions.rationale: NCI PDQ includes AFP, beta-hCG and LDH in staging/risk assessment; these markers complement rather than replace imaging, histology and appropriate specialist assessment.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABU core domain; source mapping as cited

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner is comparing a benign renal cystic lesion and an enhancing solid renal mass. Which principle is correct?

options.text: Apply PI-RADS to classify renal lesions
Use a renal-mass framework and imaging/pathology context; PI-RADS is a prostate system
Use LI-RADS, a liver system, for renal cysts
Every cyst is malignant
Imaging alone always establishes histology

practiceQuestions.rationale: Renal masses require kidney-specific classification and risk evaluation; PI-RADS is for prostate MRI and LI-RADS for liver imaging. The curriculum intentionally avoids system transfer.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABU core domain; source mapping as cited

practiceQuestions.stem: A child has antenatal hydronephrosis identified on ultrasound. Which framing is appropriate?

options.text: Adult stone algorithms apply unchanged
Age-specific evaluation and follow-up depend on severity, anatomy and clinical context; a finding alone does not determine intervention
All cases require immediate surgery
Hydronephrosis always means infection
Ignore renal function

practiceQuestions.rationale: Pediatric anatomy and risk differ. Evaluate severity, cause, infection/renal function and follow-up through age-appropriate guidance; no single image finding independently specifies treatment.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABU core domain; source mapping as cited

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about ABU initial certification is accurate according to the board’s published pathway?

options.text: This self-study course confers eligibility
Qualifying Part 1 is the only certification step
Eligible candidates must meet training/board rules and complete Part 1 and subsequent requirements including oral Part 2; this curriculum does not confer eligibility
A matching interview creates eligibility
Passing this quiz guarantees board passage

practiceQuestions.rationale: The ABU describes qualifying and certifying examinations and prerequisite training/licensure/practice requirements. Eligibility is determined solely by the board; course completion does not replace those requirements.
practiceQuestions.domain: ABU core domain; source mapping as cited

title: Vitreoretinal Surgery Fellowship

prerequisites.level: Advanced independent study for physicians who have completed ophthalmology residency or learners with equivalent supervised ophthalmic foundations; not admission or eligibility advice.
expectedKnowledge: Basic ophthalmic examination and emergency recognition
prerequisites.notProvided: No clinical supervision, patient access, simulation lab, wet lab, procedural sign-off, operative log, clinical rotation, credential or individualized advice.

objectives: Classify retinal detachment mechanisms and use a source-backed approach to emergency symptoms, examination questions, and imaging limits.
Integrate retinal anatomy, OCT/angiography/ultrasonography and findings into cautious diagnostic reasoning.
Compare the clinical reasoning domains of rhegmatogenous detachment repair, diabetic traction, PVR, macular surgery and medical-retina interfaces without asserting one operation fits all.
Recognize emergency posterior uveitis/endophthalmitis and explain urgent specialist escalation without issuing treatment orders.
Appraise open clinical evidence, guideline currency, outcomes and complication claims; document uncertainty and source limitations.
Map work to the ABO general ophthalmology 2026 WQE domains and oral-reasoning purpose, while distinguishing fellowship compliance from board certification.

units.title: Posterior-segment anatomy, ocular examination and emergency localization
objectives: Describe vitreoretinal anatomy relevant to detachment and vitreous surgery.
Build a focused history and examination that localizes posterior segment pathology and identifies urgent symptoms.
Communicate uncertainty and limitations in media-obscured examinations.
units.topics: Retina/vitreous interface, macula and fovea, PVD, RPE/choroid, ocular exam, visual acuity, pupils, dilated peripheral exam and red flags.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors—presentation/basic science; cross-domain patient safety

units.prerequisites: Ophthalmology residency-level fundamentals; this independent course does not replace supervised fellowship training.

units.title: Multimodal imaging and diagnostic reasoning
objectives: Choose an imaging modality to address a defined clinical question.
Integrate OCT, fundus photography, angiography and B-scan without treating images as stand-alone diagnoses.
State technical limits and alternative explanations.

boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors—diagnostic testing; patient safety/diagnostic error

units.prerequisites: Ophthalmology residency-level fundamentals; this independent course does not replace supervised fellowship training.

units.title: Acute PVD, retinal tears, lattice and time-sensitive triage
objectives: Distinguish uncomplicated symptoms from findings that raise concern for retinal break.
Summarize current PPP guidance on acute tears and follow-up after acute PVD without a break.
Identify symptoms requiring immediate real-world ophthalmic evaluation.
units.topics: PVD, retinal holes/tears, vitreous pigment/hemorrhage, lattice degeneration and follow-up.
boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors—presentation, diagnostic testing and management
units.casePractice: Fictional symptoms-to-triage exercise; learner supports urgency and return precautions from 2024 PPP, without suggesting remote diagnosis.

units.title: Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment and repair concepts
objectives: Explain the break–fluid mechanism and macular-status terminology.
Compare pneumatic retinopexy, scleral buckle and vitrectomy as decision frameworks, not universal algorithms.
Describe major tamponade-related counseling issues and postoperative variables at a conceptual level.

boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors—presentation, diagnostics, management/outcomes/complications
units.casePractice: Compare two fictional anatomy descriptions using a published guideline and list what cannot be determined from text alone.
units.assessment: Decision memo with alternatives and risks; rubric: anatomy 25%, evidence 35%, no false certainty 25%, follow-up/safety 15%.
units.prerequisites: Ophthalmology residency-level fundamentals; this independent course does not replace supervised fellowship training.

units.title: Proliferative vitreoretinopathy and recurrent detachment
objectives: Define PVR pathobiology and common surgical failure mechanisms.
Recognize uncertainty in recurrence prevention and distinguish established care from investigational adjuncts.
Structure a problem representation for complex recurrent detachment.

units.prerequisites: Ophthalmology residency-level fundamentals; this independent course does not replace supervised fellowship training.

units.title: Diabetic retinopathy, DME and tractional retinal detachment
objectives: Classify proliferative disease and recognize DME versus fibrovascular traction as distinct surgical contexts.
Summarize current DR PPP treatment concepts and the role of vitrectomy in selected complications.
Explain the need for individualized decisions, perioperative systemic context and safety planning.
units.topics: DR staging, PRP/anti-VEGF, DME, vitreous hemorrhage, tractional/combined detachment, surgical complications and outcomes.

units.assessment: Guideline comparison brief; rubric: stratification 30%, indication caveats 30%, complications 25%, citations 15%.
units.prerequisites: Ophthalmology residency-level fundamentals; this independent course does not replace supervised fellowship training.

units.title: Vitreomacular interface and macular surgery concepts

Interpret relevant OCT patterns and identify decision variables for referral/specialist discussion.
Describe outcome uncertainty and risks without teaching operative competence.

units.prerequisites: Ophthalmology residency-level fundamentals; this independent course does not replace supervised fellowship training.

units.title: Medical retina foundation for vitreoretinal surgeons: AMD and vascular disease
objectives: Compare major AMD phenotypes and retinal vascular disease patterns at the overview level.
Interpret current public guidance without extrapolating simplified public education into patient-specific treatment.
Summarize outcome and adherence variables in longitudinal care.

boardDomains: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors—macular and vascular diseases

units.title: Uveitis, diagnostic vitrectomy and infectious endophthalmitis
objectives: Recognize when posterior inflammation/infection is urgent and requires immediate specialist evaluation.
Describe diagnostic sampling concepts and limitations of post-procedure endophthalmitis evidence.
Differentiate educational reasoning from prescribing or authorizing treatment.

units.casePractice: Read the open clinical-practice update; give a fictional time-critical communication plan rather than a medication order.

units.prerequisites: Ophthalmology residency-level fundamentals; this independent course does not replace supervised fellowship training.

units.title: Pediatric retina, ROP and inherited disease
objectives: Describe key pediatric vitreoretinal referral contexts and why adult patterns may not transfer.
Summarize ROP and inherited retinal/choroidal disease as board-level domains.
Identify potential genetic counseling and multidisciplinary interfaces.

units.prerequisites: Ophthalmology residency-level fundamentals; this independent course does not replace supervised fellowship training.

objectives: Identify posterior-segment trauma and foreign-body contexts requiring emergency systems and team coordination.

Distinguish ocular melanoma diagnostic evaluation from nonspecific retinal lesions.

units.prerequisites: Ophthalmology residency-level fundamentals; this independent course does not replace supervised fellowship training.

objectives: Explain the educational limits of surgical videos and why supervised deliberate practice is essential.

Map outcome/QI, complications, consent and professionalism to the ophthalmology board domains.
units.topics: Case selection, informed consent, tamponade counseling, complications, learning curves, research ethics, trials, outcomes/QI and safety.

assignment.title: Retina reasoning and evidence portfolio
deliverables: A source-linked triage and missing-data analysis for one fictional RRD vignette.
A one-page multimodal imaging question/limitations matrix.
A diabetic retinopathy or PVR guideline/evidence appraisal with publication date and population qualifiers.
A brief oral-style case presentation with differential, evidence, risk/unknowns and a question for supervising clinician.
A patient-image provenance and reuse checklist: link only unless a specific license permits a proposed use.
assignment.policy: All constructed cases are explicitly fictional; do not use actual patient records or copy/rehost protected images. No treatment plan or procedure permission is produced.

formative: 10 original source-cited, board-style educational questions in this package (not ABO material).

mapping.institution: Mass Eye and Ear / Harvard Medical School
mapping.name: Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary Vitreoretinal Fellowship
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: The official MEE page calls it a two-year, AUPO FCC-compliant clinical fellowship; medical/surgical retina objectives; named scope includes RRD, diabetic TRD, PVR, macular surgery, traumatic detachment/IOFB, dislocated lenses/scleral-fixated IOLs, KPro, ocular oncology and pediatric retina. Fellows participate in pre/intra/postoperative care, call and research; public page does not provide a complete lecture list, exact fellow operative volume or detailed rotation schedule. AUPO directory snapshot lists “Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary Vitreoretinal Fellowship,” Harvard Medical School, next review 2027, four positions. No ACGME retina fellowship accreditation statement found.

mapping.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions (Wilmer Eye Institute)
mapping.name: Medical and Surgical Retina Advanced Specialty Training (Wilmer Retina Advanced Specialty Training Fellowship)
mapping.publicCurriculumNotes: Official Wilmer page titles the programme “Medical and Surgical Retina Advanced Specialty Training” and describes a two-year AUPO FCC-compliant clinical fellowship training in medical and surgical retina. It states expected competencies but not a week-by-week curriculum or exact rotations/case volume. Page states some IMG-specific prerequisites (completed ophthalmology residency, ECFMG, USMLE, Maryland licensure and H-1B eligibility); these are explicitly for international graduates and not generalized to all applicants. AUPO directory listing uses exact institution label “Johns Hopkins School of Medicine,” sponsoring institution “Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions,” next review 2028, two positions.

unitMap.text: Posterior-segment anatomy, ocular examination and emergency localization
Multimodal imaging and diagnostic reasoning
Acute PVD, retinal tears, lattice and time-sensitive triage
Rhegmatogenous retinal detachment and repair concepts
Proliferative vitreoretinopathy and recurrent detachment
Diabetic retinopathy, DME and tractional retinal detachment
Vitreomacular interface and macular surgery concepts
Medical retina foundation for vitreoretinal surgeons: AMD and vascular disease
Uveitis, diagnostic vitrectomy and infectious endophthalmitis
Pediatric retina, ROP and inherited disease
Ocular trauma, foreign body, dislocated lens and ocular oncology interfaces
Surgical safety, perioperative systems, research and outcomes

topicGaps: The unique public lecture ledger now contains 46 recordings with observed runtimes, totalling 28.460000 free hours. The 36-hour video target remains unmet by 7.540000 hours (452.4 minutes); no planned/scripted minutes count toward this total.

Added specialist recordings broaden coverage in diabetic vitrectomy, retinal-detachment repair/PVR, acute tear/floaters reasoning, OCT interpretation, uveitis diagnostic work-up and open-globe trauma. They are educational recordings, not supervised surgical training or patient-specific guidance.

Clinical procedural judgment and operative skills, case selection, complication management, supervised operative volume, postoperative follow-up and institutional emergency systems remain unavailable through self-study and underrepresented in public didactics. The MEE and Wilmer public pages do not publish full lecture sets or exact case volumes.

Current, in-depth PVR recurrence/prevention evidence, detailed pediatric retina/ROP care, inherited retinal disease/genetics, complex ocular oncology, lens/IOL and KPro interfaces, and specialty-level outcomes/QI still lack enough verified free recorded instruction in this packet. A public 2025 ROP lecture and several newer ophthalmology recordings had no observed usable duration and remain uncounted.

AAO PPP and clinical evidence must be checked for updates. Older webinars (including the 2017 uveitis diagnostic recording and 2018 diabetic-surgery talk) are useful historical teaching inputs, not current treatment directives; contentious speaker opinions are not elevated to guideline recommendations.

The 33 pre-existing originalClipPlan entries total 965 planned target minutes. Those targets remain estimates, are not rendered media, and predate this expansion; they do not erase the 452.4-minute verified residual gap or establish production feasibility.

boardNames: American Board of Ophthalmology (ABO)—general ophthalmology initial certification; Written Qualifying Examination (WQE) and Oral Examination. No separate U.S. vitreoretinal subspecialty board examination/certificate identified in official ABO materials reviewed.
medical.boardStatus: The relevant U.S. primary specialty certifier is the American Board of Ophthalmology. Official ABO pages describe general ophthalmology certification after accredited residency via WQE and oral examination. No separate U.S. vitreoretinal fellowship board examination or subspecialty certificate was identified in official ABO materials reviewed (checked 2026-10-07). AUPO FCC compliance is a fellowship training-compliance process, not board certification. The general ophthalmology WQE 2026 outline weights Retina, Vitreous and Intraocular Tumors at 15%; this is not a fellowship-specific exam blueprint.
medical.boardEligibilityNotice: Educational mapping only. This independent course does not confer ABO exam eligibility or board status. ABO eligibility requires applicable accredited ophthalmology residency and current ABO rules; verify directly with ABO. Each institution has its own match, prerequisite, state medical-license and visa requirements; do not infer universal eligibility from this course. MEE page says applicants must be eligible for a full Massachusetts medical license. Wilmer page enumerates separate IMG prerequisites only.

officialProgrammes.institution: Mass Eye and Ear / Harvard Medical School
officialProgrammes.name: Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary Vitreoretinal Fellowship
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: The official MEE page calls it a two-year, AUPO FCC-compliant clinical fellowship; medical/surgical retina objectives; named scope includes RRD, diabetic TRD, PVR, macular surgery, traumatic detachment/IOFB, dislocated lenses/scleral-fixated IOLs, KPro, ocular oncology and pediatric retina. Fellows participate in pre/intra/postoperative care, call and research; public page does not provide a complete lecture list, exact fellow operative volume or detailed rotation schedule. AUPO directory snapshot lists “Massachusetts Eye and Ear Infirmary Vitreoretinal Fellowship,” Harvard Medical School, next review 2027, four positions. No ACGME retina fellowship accreditation statement found.

officialProgrammes.institution: Johns Hopkins School of Medicine / Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions (Wilmer Eye Institute)
officialProgrammes.name: Medical and Surgical Retina Advanced Specialty Training (Wilmer Retina Advanced Specialty Training Fellowship)
officialProgrammes.publicCurriculumNotes: Official Wilmer page titles the programme “Medical and Surgical Retina Advanced Specialty Training” and describes a two-year AUPO FCC-compliant clinical fellowship training in medical and surgical retina. It states expected competencies but not a week-by-week curriculum or exact rotations/case volume. Page states some IMG-specific prerequisites (completed ophthalmology residency, ECFMG, USMLE, Maryland licensure and H-1B eligibility); these are explicitly for international graduates and not generalized to all applicants. AUPO directory listing uses exact institution label “Johns Hopkins School of Medicine,” sponsoring institution “Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions,” next review 2028, two positions.

medical.programmeSourceScope: The packet originally named MEE only. Independent verification additionally found a distinct Johns Hopkins Wilmer clinical Medical and Surgical Retina Advanced Specialty Training fellowship. Exact programme names are retained separately. Both are clinical physician fellowship tracks and AUPO FCC-compliant, not an ACGME-accredited retina fellowship according to the pages reviewed. ACGME publishes requirements for ophthalmology residency and ophthalmic plastic/reconstructive fellowship; that does not establish ACGME accreditation of the retina fellowships. MEE page describes operative/medical retina/call/research experiences and the separate annual vitrectomy course. Hopkins describes two-year medical/surgical competencies, clinical participation, education, clinical trials/research and call content under navigable headings; no complete public rotation schedule or proprietary lecture set was accessible. No research-only/non-physician track or generic directory-only category is substituted for these two clinical programmes.
sourceCaveats: Institutional fellowship descriptions are self-reported public descriptions and are not an independently observed curriculum, operative-volume audit, or accreditation determination. AUPO FCC compliance and ACGME accreditation are distinct.
The 2019 AUPO program requirements PDF is a dated source. The current AUPO listing page gave review dates, but no revised PDF version was confirmed in this review.

ABO content outline is effective for 2026, includes nine weighted general specialty domains, and is explicitly a study outline rather than a study guide; do not mislabel it as retina-fellowship blueprint.

Clinical sources may update after the date checked; AAO guideline links should be checked for latest version before any clinical discussion. Public education does not provide patient-specific care advice.

A YouTube playlist/video may be changed, removed, geoblocked or made private. Durations were checked anonymously at the date of metadata retrieval; visit original URLs. Publication dates were not present in the collected flat metadata, so are null except dates visible in titles.

topicGaps: The unique public lecture ledger now contains 46 recordings with observed runtimes, totalling 28.460000 free hours. The 36-hour video target remains unmet by 7.540000 hours (452.4 minutes); no planned/scripted minutes count toward this total.

Added specialist recordings broaden coverage in diabetic vitrectomy, retinal-detachment repair/PVR, acute tear/floaters reasoning, OCT interpretation, uveitis diagnostic work-up and open-globe trauma. They are educational recordings, not supervised surgical training or patient-specific guidance.

Clinical procedural judgment and operative skills, case selection, complication management, supervised operative volume, postoperative follow-up and institutional emergency systems remain unavailable through self-study and underrepresented in public didactics. The MEE and Wilmer public pages do not publish full lecture sets or exact case volumes.

Current, in-depth PVR recurrence/prevention evidence, detailed pediatric retina/ROP care, inherited retinal disease/genetics, complex ocular oncology, lens/IOL and KPro interfaces, and specialty-level outcomes/QI still lack enough verified free recorded instruction in this packet. A public 2025 ROP lecture and several newer ophthalmology recordings had no observed usable duration and remain uncounted.

AAO PPP and clinical evidence must be checked for updates. Older webinars (including the 2017 uveitis diagnostic recording and 2018 diabetic-surgery talk) are useful historical teaching inputs, not current treatment directives; contentious speaker opinions are not elevated to guideline recommendations.

The 33 pre-existing originalClipPlan entries total 965 planned target minutes. Those targets remain estimates, are not rendered media, and predate this expansion; they do not erase the 452.4-minute verified residual gap or establish production feasibility.

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional adult reports new flashes, a shower of floaters and a dark curtain. No examination is available. What is the most defensible next statement?

options.text: Call this a proven rhegmatogenous detachment and choose vitrectomy
Possible retinal detachment is an urgent ophthalmic problem requiring prompt in-person assessment
Wait for symptoms to resolve because pain is absent
Start anti-VEGF treatment based on symptoms

practiceQuestions.rationale: The symptom pattern is concerning and requires urgent ophthalmic evaluation; symptoms alone do not establish detachment subtype or operation.
practiceQuestions.domain: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors—presentation, diagnostic testing and management

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional patient has an acute symptomatic horseshoe tear documented on exam. Which guideline-level statement is most accurate?

options.text: Acute horseshoe tears usually require treatment
All asymptomatic lattice lesions must be lasered
All acute PVD without a break requires surgery
No retinal break requires treatment

practiceQuestions.rationale: The AAO PPP highlights that acute horseshoe tears and traumatic retinal breaks usually require treatment; other lesions require individualized assessment.
practiceQuestions.domain: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors—presentation, diagnostic testing and management

practiceQuestions.stem: Which mechanism best defines a rhegmatogenous retinal detachment?

options.text: Fluid accumulation without a break from exudation
Fibrovascular membrane contraction only
A retinal break permits vitreous fluid to pass beneath neurosensory retina
Optic nerve swelling elevates retina

practiceQuestions.rationale: RRD is associated with a full-thickness retinal break through which liquefied vitreous can enter the subretinal space.
practiceQuestions.domain: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors—presentation, diagnostics, management/outcomes/complications

practiceQuestions.stem: In a media-obscured eye where the posterior fundus cannot be visualized, which study can help assess for a detachment?

options.text: B-scan ocular ultrasonography
Automated perimetry only
Color vision plate only
Corneal topography

practiceQuestions.rationale: B-scan ultrasound may help evaluate posterior-segment anatomy when the media is opaque; it complements rather than replaces clinical assessment.
practiceQuestions.domain: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors—presentation, diagnostic testing and management

practiceQuestions.stem: A fictional eye has proliferative diabetic retinopathy, fibrovascular traction threatening the macula, and vitreous hemorrhage. Which description is most appropriate?

options.text: This is necessarily a simple nontractional macular-edema case
Tractional or combined disease is a recognized context in which vitreoretinal surgery may be considered by a specialist
It proves every PDR eye needs immediate vitrectomy
A retinal break must be present in every tractional detachment

practiceQuestions.rationale: The NEI distinguishes tractional detachment caused by scarring from break-mediated RRD, and an open review describes selected diabetic vitrectomy indications; decisions depend on case-specific specialist evaluation.
practiceQuestions.domain: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors; Pediatric retinal disorders is not this unit

practiceQuestions.stem: Which statement about PVR is best supported by the cited review?

options.text: It is an inflammatory/wound-healing response with membrane formation and contraction; no proven pharmacologic preventive agent was identified in that review
It is always prevented by small-gauge instruments
It is a synonym for macular edema
Anti-VEGF is proven to prevent PVR in all detachments

practiceQuestions.rationale: The open review describes cellular membrane growth/contraction as abnormal wound healing and notes surgery as management, with no proven preventive drug at publication.
practiceQuestions.domain: Retina, Vitreous, and Intraocular Tumors—pathophysiology, management/outcomes/complications

practiceQuestions.stem: A learner sees an OCT image showing fluid. Which approach is most appropriate?

options.text: Infer one diagnosis without clinical context
Ask what clinical question the OCT can address and interpret it with exam and other modalities
Use OCT alone to rule out peripheral tears
Assume all subretinal fluid indicates AMD

practiceQuestions.rationale: Imaging interpretation requires clinical correlation and modality limitations; OCT does not replace peripheral examination for retinal breaks.

Schedule routine follow-up in several weeks
Reassure because infection is rare
Use a remote image to prescribe treatment

practiceQuestions.stem: Which is the official U.S. certifying board and pathway identified for a retina-trained ophthalmologist?

options.text: Separate American Board of Vitreoretinal Surgery exam only
ABO general ophthalmology initial certification uses WQE and oral exam after accredited ophthalmology residency; no separate retina board exam identified

ACGME certifies retina specialists by written retina examination
